meta.abstract: Vertiv Holdings Co (VRT, NYSE) is the Westerville, Ohio-headquartered designer, manufacturer, and services provider of the critical infrastructure that makes data centres operable — uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), power distribution units (PDU), thermal management systems (chillers, computer room air conditioners, liquid-cooling solutions), monitoring and management software, and the integrated services that the major hyperscaler and enterprise IT data centre buildouts require at scale. The company traces its corporate ancestry to the 1965 founding of Liebert Corporation as a precision cooling specialist for early mainframe computers; through five decades of acquisitions and ownership transitions the business became Emerson Network Power, then was carved out by Emerson Electric in November 2016 to private equity (Platinum Equity at the time of carve-out, then sold to investor consortium including Goldman Sachs Asset Management) for approximately $4 billion, and listed publicly via a SPAC business combination with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp in February 2020. CEO Giordano (Gio) Albertazzi was named to the role effective January 1, 2023 succeeding Rob Johnson; Albertazzi had been President of the Americas region before the CEO promotion. The strategic operating story of the post-2023 period has been the AI data centre infrastructure capex cycle that has made high-density liquid-cooling solutions, switchgear for multi-megawatt power deployments, and the integrated full-stack data centre infrastructure offering structurally central to the hyperscaler buildout. FY2025 (the calendar year) produced revenue of approximately $9.0-9.5 billion (the precise figure in the 10-K filed February 2026), an exit-year organic order growth rate that management has characterised as substantially above the broader industry, and adjusted operating margins expanding into the high-teens percentage range. The board is chaired by David Cote (former Honeywell Chairman and CEO, who also chairs the related GS Acquisition transactions) and includes a slate of directors with deep industrial-equipment, private-equity, and technology-industry experience. The investment proposition compresses the AI capex sustainability, the structural advantage of being one of the two-or-three meaningful global suppliers of full-stack data centre infrastructure (alongside Schneider Electric and Eaton), the liquid-cooling product cycle that has been the highest-growth single product category, and the operating leverage as the post-SPAC capital structure continues compressing toward an investment-grade profile.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Between 2022 and 2024, Vertiv Holdings executed one of the more remarkable margin recoveries in U.S. industrial technology. Adjusted operating profit margin expanded from approximately 6% to 19.4%, while revenue climbed from $5.69 billion to $8.01 billion. The driver was AI: as Nvidia H100 and H200 server configurations concentrated power above 30–40 kilowatts per rack — beyond the thermal ceiling of conventional computer-room air handling — hyperscalers began specifying liquid cooling as mandatory infrastructure. Vertiv's rear-door heat exchangers and direct-to-chip cold plates, niche products through the 2010s, became central to the largest capital programmes in technology history.

Vertiv Holdings ([VRT, NYSE](https://investors.vertiv.com/)), headquartered in Westerville, Ohio, supplies mission-critical data centre infrastructure: thermal management (liquid cooling, CRAH/CRAC, free cooling chillers), power management (Liebert-branded UPS systems, switchgear, busway, PDUs), IT racks and enclosures, and lifecycle services. The company serves hyperscalers — Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta — alongside colocation operators including Equinix and Digital Realty, and enterprise data centre operators globally. Revenue is reported across three segments: Americas (the largest by revenue), Asia Pacific, and EMEA, with the Americas the principal beneficiary of the AI infrastructure cycle.

## Leadership and Origins

Vertiv's current form traces to December 2016, when Emerson Electric divested its Network Power division to Platinum Equity for approximately $4 billion, rebranding it as Vertiv. In February 2020, the company went public through a SPAC merger with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp, a vehicle chaired by David Cote — former Chairman and CEO of Honeywell International and the most consequential U.S. industrial-equipment CEO of his generation. Cote remains Vertiv's non-executive Chairman; Jacob Kotzubei of Platinum Equity continues to sit on the board, preserving the carve-out era's institutional memory.

Giordano (Gio) Albertazzi became Chief Executive Officer on January 1, 2023, succeeding Rob Johnson. Albertazzi had previously run the Americas region, the company's largest business unit, and his operational depth across the product portfolio and hyperscaler customer relationships has underpinned execution through the AI demand inflection. David Fallon, who joined as CFO in 2017 and stewarded Vertiv through the SPAC listing, the post-listing deleveraging, and the dividend initiation, announced his retirement in May 2025; Craig Chamberlain succeeded him as CFO later that year.

## Financial Baseline

The compounding through the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026 reflects acceleration across revenue, margin, and order intake that few industrial-technology peers have matched in the same window.

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.69B | $6.86B | $8.01B | $10.20B |
| Adj. Operating Margin | ~6.0% | ~14.4% | ~19.4% | ~20.4% |
| Adj. Diluted EPS | — | — | ~$2.86 | $4.20 |

[Source: Vertiv Q4 2025 earnings press release; SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101)

Orders growth has materially outpaced revenue throughout the cycle. By Q4 2025, the [backlog reached $15 billion](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/02/11/vertiv-vrt-q4-2025-earnings-call-transcript/) — more than double the prior year's figure and up 57% sequentially from Q3's $9.5 billion — as organic orders grew 152% year-over-year in the quarter alone. On the February 2026 earnings call, Albertazzi was direct about the pipeline's condition behind the headline backlog number:

> "The pipeline has not depleted. If anything, despite the very strong order intake in the last quarter, we have seen the pipeline to grow quarter to quarter."

For FY2026, Vertiv guided to net sales of $13.25–$13.75 billion and adjusted operating margin of 22.5% — 210 basis points of additional expansion on a revenue base roughly 2.3 times the 2022 level.

## Liquid Cooling Portfolio

Vertiv's liquid cooling range spans the density spectrum from legacy mixed-use facilities to purpose-built AI factories. Rear-door heat exchangers and in-row coolant distribution units address lower-density deployments. Direct-to-chip cold plates, delivered through the CoolChip CDU family, address AI configurations above the air-cooling threshold — with capacity running from 70 kilowatts to 2,300 kilowatts per unit. The [CoolChip CDU 2300](https://www.vertiv.com/en-us/about/news-and-events/corporate-news/vertiv-expands-its-global-liquid-cooling-portfolio-with-the-announcement-of-two-new-high-capacity-coolant-distribution-units-to-support-ai-applications/), announced at SC24 in November 2024, is a liquid-to-liquid unit Vertiv positioned as the highest-capacity CDU per square foot available.

The [CoolPhase Flex](https://www.vertiv.com/en-us/campaigns/vertiv-coolphase-flex-packaged-system/), launched commercially in 2025, is a hybrid air/liquid packaged system convertible between cooling modes in the field in approximately four hours — addressing operators managing mixed-density environments during the rack-power transition. In November 2025, Vertiv announced the acquisition of [PurgeRite](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/vertiv-announces-intent-to-acquire-purgerite-a-leading-provider-of-specialized-fluid-management-services-to-expand-liquid-cooling-services-portfolio-302602394.html), a Houston-based specialist in mechanical flushing and filtration services for liquid-cooled data centres, for approximately $1.0 billion cash plus up to $250 million in earnout — extending the liquid cooling proposition from equipment manufacturing into recurring services revenue.

## The Central Tension

As of the snapshot date, Vertiv's market capitalisation stood at approximately $125 billion, from roughly $42 billion at the close of 2024 — a re-rating that prices in a sustained AI infrastructure capex cycle extending well beyond the near-term backlog horizon.

The dossier's animating questions follow directly: how durable is the AI infrastructure build-out as hyperscaler deployment shifts toward inference, as future accelerator generations potentially compress per-rack power requirements, or as macro conditions alter capex plans? What is Vertiv's competitive position against Schneider Electric, Eaton, Trane Technologies, and liquid cooling pure-plays in a thermal management market where entry barriers are meaningfully lower than in high-voltage power? And can the adjusted operating margin sustain further expansion as revenue approaches $13.5 billion — Vertiv's own guidance midpoint — without the mix tailwinds that drove the initial recovery? The chapters that follow take each question in turn.

chapters.title: From Emerson Network Power to Platinum, GS Acquisition SPAC, and the AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The Network Power Division: Emerson Electric's Data Centre Decade

For roughly three decades, what would eventually become Vertiv operated as a division within Emerson Electric Co., the St. Louis-based industrial conglomerate. Emerson's Network Power segment supplied mission-critical infrastructure to data centres, telecommunications facilities, and industrial installations worldwide. The portfolio had been assembled through targeted acquisitions: the Liebert Corporation, absorbed in 1987, provided uninterruptible power supply systems that became the backbone of enterprise data centre power chains; ASCO Power Technologies added automatic transfer switches and switchgear; Avocent Corporation, acquired in 2009 for approximately $1.2 billion, contributed IT management software and remote-access infrastructure.

By the early 2010s, Network Power was generating revenues in the range of $4 to $5 billion annually — substantial by any measure, but structurally different from Emerson's core automation-and-controls businesses. CEO David Farr had concluded that the company's defensible long-cycle moat resided in Process Management and Industrial Automation, not in a business exposed to the shorter product cycles and hyperscaler customer dynamics of data centre infrastructure. Beginning in 2014, Farr communicated the strategic rationale for concentrating around the automation core and divesting the Network Power and Tools & Storage segments. The formal divestiture process for Network Power launched in 2015.

## The Platinum Equity Carve-Out: December 2016

The transaction closed in December 2016. [Platinum Equity](https://www.platinumequity.com/), the Beverly Hills-based private equity firm led by Tom Gores, acquired the Emerson Network Power business for approximately $4 billion in enterprise value. The business was renamed Vertiv Holdings, a rebrand intended to signal independence from the Emerson corporate identity and a focus on the criticality of data centre infrastructure as a standalone category.

Platinum Equity's model is built around carve-out operational restructuring. At Vertiv, the programme included rationalising a global manufacturing footprint that had accumulated across decades of conglomerate ownership, standardising procurement and supply-chain processes, and reorienting the commercial organisation toward the hyperscaler and colocation segments posting the fastest demand growth. Jacob Kotzubei, Co-President of Platinum Equity, joined the Vertiv board — a seat he retained through the SPAC era and the subsequent public-company period, providing private-equity operating continuity across the governance structure.

## The GS Acquisition SPAC and the Cote Partnership: February 2020

The vehicle that brought Vertiv to public markets was GS Acquisition Holdings Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by David M. Cote. Cote had served as Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Honeywell International from 2002 to 2017 — a tenure that produced one of the most closely studied operational transformations in US large-cap industrial history, including the Honeywell Operating System and a compound total-shareholder return that substantially outperformed the industrial sector over fifteen years. His association with the Vertiv listing carried meaningful signal: a SPAC sponsored by the most prominent US industrial chief executive of his generation, taking public a data centre infrastructure business at what was already, by late 2019, a visible inflection in the hyperscaler capex cycle.

The business combination between GS Acquisition Holdings Corp and Vertiv closed on [February 7, 2020](https://investors.vertiv.com/), with common stock commencing trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker VRT. Cote assumed the chairmanship of the combined public company. The post-SPAC board was assembled with deliberate governance depth: Roger Fradin, a former Vice Chairman of Honeywell who ran Automation and Control Solutions through the Cote era; Edward L. Monser, the former Chief Operating Officer of Emerson Electric, providing institutional memory of the carve-out business; and Kotzubei retaining his Platinum seat. The timing, however, was adversarial. The combination closed weeks before the COVID-19 pandemic imposed a global demand shock, and Vertiv shares traded weakly through the spring and summer of 2020 as the market processed the pandemic's implications for enterprise capital expenditure.

## The Rob Johnson Era: Post-SPAC Establishment and Supply-Chain Pressure

Rob Johnson served as Chief Executive Officer from the SPAC listing through late 2022, guiding Vertiv through the post-merger integration and the difficult macroeconomic environment of the pandemic period. The Johnson era was defined by two compounding structural challenges: the global supply-chain disruptions of 2021-2022, which drove input-cost inflation in components, copper, and logistics faster than pricing could adjust; and the residual integration inefficiencies of a business that had moved, within four years, from conglomerate subsidiary to private-equity portfolio company to listed industrial technology group.

By fiscal year 2022, Vertiv reported revenues of approximately $5.69 billion — a business of meaningful scale, but one generating an adjusted operating profit margin of approximately 6 percent. The margin underperformance relative to peers reflected both the supply-chain headwinds of the period and an operational programme that had not yet fully resolved the cost-structure legacy of the carve-out years. The equity, despite its sponsorship pedigree and an accelerating AI data centre demand signal visible in late 2022, had not produced the re-rating the board's industrial pedigree implied.

## The Albertazzi Succession: January 2023

Giordano Albertazzi — universally known within Vertiv as Gio — assumed the chief executive role effective January 1, 2023, succeeding Johnson. Albertazzi had joined the Vertiv organisation through the Emerson Network Power lineage and had served most recently as Chief Executive Officer of Vertiv's EMEA region. His promotion from regional general management rather than from an external search was a deliberate signal from the board: the 2023 challenge was operational execution, not strategic reinvention, and an executive who understood the product portfolio, the manufacturing operations, and the customer relationships from the inside was the appropriate choice for what was already visible as an accelerating demand environment.

Albertazzi moved quickly to tighten operational execution across the global organisation. CFO David Fallon, in post since 2017 — predating the SPAC listing and providing financial continuity across the Platinum ownership and public-company periods — remained in place through the transition, a structural advantage for a company executing complex multi-year deleveraging, dividend initiation, and share repurchase programmes simultaneously.

The adjusted operating margin expanded from approximately 6 percent in 2022 to approximately 14.4 percent in 2023 — an eight-percentage-point improvement within a single fiscal year that stands as one of the more consequential margin recoveries in US industrial-technology equipment during the period. It would not be the ceiling.

## The AI Liquid Cooling Inflection: 2023–2025

The demand catalyst that amplified Albertazzi's operational improvements into a structural re-rating was the artificial intelligence data centre buildout. Beginning in earnest in 2023 and accelerating through 2024 and 2025, the capital expenditure programmes of Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, and Meta drove a step-change in the power density requirements of data centre rack configurations. Nvidia's H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU architectures — optimised for large-scale AI training and inference — require rack power densities in the range of 30 to 100 kilowatts per rack, well above the approximately 10-to-15 kilowatts that traditional air-cooling infrastructure can reliably manage.

Vertiv's liquid cooling portfolio became essential infrastructure for any high-density AI deployment: direct-to-chip cold plates that circulate coolant directly across GPU heat spreaders, rear-door heat exchangers that capture heat at the rack exit, and coolant distribution units that manage the broader facility loop. The company's Liebert-brand power management systems — high-efficiency UPS platforms, precision power distribution units, and switchgear — similarly benefited from the density increase: more power per rack means more power infrastructure per unit of floor space.

The financial result is visible in the reported metrics across the three-year period:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Adj. Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $5.69B | ~6.0% |
| 2023 | $6.86B | ~14.4% |
| 2024 | $8.01B | ~19.4% |

*Sources: [Vertiv Investor Relations](https://investors.vertiv.com/); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101)*

Revenue grew at a compound annual rate of approximately 19 percent across the 2022-to-2024 period. Critically, orders growth materially outpaced revenue growth across 2023-2025, as hyperscalers committed to multi-year AI infrastructure programmes that populated Vertiv's backlog well ahead of revenue recognition — a structural demand signal that implied sustained growth extending across multiple forward fiscal years.

## An AI Infrastructure Pure-Play, Built From a Conglomerate Division

The decade separating Emerson's divestiture decision from Vertiv's fiscal year 2024 results produced a transformation that few carve-out histories can match in its combination of scale, margin, and strategic positioning. What had been valued at approximately $4 billion at the 2016 carve-out — a capable but suboptimally operated conglomerate division — had, through four distinct ownership and management phases, become one of the most directly positioned AI data centre infrastructure equities available in US public markets.

As Vertiv exited 2024, the company carried approximately $8.0 billion in annual revenue, a 19-percent adjusted operating margin, a substantial orders backlog anchored by hyperscaler multi-year commitments, and a board whose industrial-equipment governance depth — the Honeywell-Emerson-Platinum pedigree concentration in Cote, Fradin, Monser, and Kotzubei — was, for a company of its market capitalisation, genuinely unusual. The Emerson carve-out, the Platinum restructuring, the Cote SPAC, and the Albertazzi succession had each contributed a necessary layer. The AI capex cycle had found the result precisely positioned to serve it.

chapters.title: Thermal management, power management, services, and the liquid cooling pivot
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of Necessity

Vertiv's commercial proposition is rooted in an immutable physics constraint: the computers inside a modern data centre generate heat that cannot be wished away. Every watt consumed becomes a watt of thermal load that the facility must shed — and as artificial intelligence drove server rack power densities from the low single-digit kilowatts of the mid-2010s through 20 kilowatts, then 40, then past 100 kilowatts per rack in the latest Nvidia Blackwell GPU configurations, the engineering solutions required underwent a categorical shift. Vertiv sells the infrastructure that bridges that shift.

The company reports geographically — Americas, Asia Pacific, and EMEA — but its product organisation divides into four functional pillars: thermal management, power management, IT racks and enclosures with associated software, and lifecycle services. Each is critical to mission-critical data centre operation. Only one is structurally re-rating in the AI era.

## Thermal Management: Where the AI Cycle Lives

Traditional data centre thermal management was built around the computer-room air handler, or CRAH — essentially a very large, very precise air conditioner. Vertiv's Liebert-branded CRAH and CRAC (computer-room air conditioner) units remain a substantial installed-base product and generate recurring replacement revenue across enterprise and colocation facilities worldwide. Free cooling chillers, which exploit ambient temperatures to reduce mechanical refrigeration load, complete the conventional air-side portfolio and are a material revenue category in temperate markets including Northern Europe.

The structural limitation of air cooling is thermodynamic and unforgiving. Air's low heat capacity means that beyond approximately 30 to 40 kilowatts per rack, conventional air management can no longer extract heat fast enough without recirculation inefficiencies that undermine the broader facility. Beyond roughly 100 kilowatts per rack — the territory Nvidia's Blackwell NVL72 and subsequent architectures occupy — air cooling is effectively non-viable regardless of airflow volume. Liquid, with its roughly 3,500 times greater volumetric heat capacity than air, is the only engineering answer.

Vertiv's liquid cooling product portfolio spans three primary form factors. Rear-door heat exchangers mount directly to the back of a standard server rack and use chilled water to capture exhaust heat before it reaches the room air; they are retrofittable into existing infrastructure and represent the lower-density entry point to liquid thermal management. In-row coolant distribution units circulate cold water through manifolds positioned between rack rows, allowing per-rack flow control and integration with building management systems. Direct-to-chip cold plates — Vertiv markets the CoolPhase platform in this category — attach physically to the processor package itself, routing chilled water within millimetres of the GPU die and achieving the heat extraction rates that high-density AI clusters demand.

> "The liquid cooling market is not a niche any more. It is becoming mainstream, and the density curves we see from our hyperscaler customers suggest this is a multi-year, structurally embedded demand cycle, not a single capex spike." — Gio Albertazzi, Q4 2024 earnings call

The physics logic maps directly to the Nvidia GPU roadmap. H100 racks operated at approximately 30 to 60 kilowatts in standard configurations; H200 pushed that envelope further. Blackwell NVL72 clusters, the current reference architecture for frontier AI training, exceed 100 kilowatts per rack in dense deployments. Each successive generation has moved more AI infrastructure across the threshold where liquid cooling transitions from optional to required, and Vertiv's direct-to-chip and rear-door products are the principal commercial beneficiaries.

The company has not disclosed liquid cooling as a standalone revenue line in its public filings, but management commentary across multiple earnings periods since 2023 has consistently characterised liquid cooling orders growth as the fastest-expanding category in the backlog — a backlog that, by the close of fiscal 2024, was itself growing materially faster than recognised revenue.

## Power Management: The Parallel Infrastructure Play

While liquid cooling draws investor attention, Vertiv's power management division represents the larger and more immediate revenue base. Every watt that must ultimately be cooled first passes through Vertiv's power chain.

The Liebert UPS (uninterruptible power supply) franchise is the cornerstone. Liebert, acquired by Emerson Electric over several decades of bolt-on transactions before the 2016 Network Power divestiture, is among the best-recognised brands in data centre power conditioning. Vertiv's UPS portfolio spans from small enterprise units to the large modular three-phase systems deployed by hyperscalers in megawatt-scale configurations. Switchgear and medium-voltage distribution equipment sits at the facility power intake, managing the transition from utility feed to internal distribution. Starline busway — a continuous-access power distribution product that allows data centres to add or relocate load without service interruptions — is a differentiated product with strong colocation and hyperscaler penetration, given its ability to support the rapid reconfiguration that AI cluster builds require. Power distribution units at the rack level complete the chain.

The power management product line benefits from the same AI capex dynamic as thermal: each new AI data centre cluster requires switchgear, UPS, busway, and PDU content that scales directly with installed GPU count. Vertiv's power content per AI rack is structurally significant relative to a conventional server configuration, because the higher absolute power loads demand more robust distribution infrastructure throughout.

## IT Racks, Enclosures, and Software

Vertiv manufactures the physical enclosure infrastructure — racks, cabinets, and containment systems — that houses servers in hyperscaler and enterprise facilities. This segment is lower-margin than power and thermal equipment but serves a key integration role: Vertiv's rack systems are increasingly designed with embedded cooling manifolds and integrated power distribution, allowing customers to procure a pre-configured, high-density compute enclosure rather than assembling components from multiple vendors. The integration thesis is commercially important for the AI data centre market, where speed of deployment is a competitive variable for hyperscalers and time-to-capacity matters.

Data centre infrastructure management software — DCIM, in industry shorthand — rounds out the category. Vertiv's software portfolio monitors power draw, thermal performance, and asset status across the facility, providing the telemetry that operators require to manage high-density environments safely. Software carries recurring license revenue characteristics and reinforces customer stickiness.

## Lifecycle Services: The Recurring Revenue Layer

Services — field maintenance, preventive maintenance contracts, remote monitoring, spare parts, and emergency response — constitute Vertiv's most predictable revenue stream and its highest-gross-margin segment. The installed base of deployed Vertiv and legacy Liebert equipment running in data centres globally creates a durable aftermarket that is largely insulated from capital expenditure cycles. When a hyperscaler defers a new facility build, it does not defer maintenance on its existing Liebert UPS fleet.

Services revenues also expand organically as the installed base grows. Each new data centre deployment — AI-driven or otherwise — that incorporates Vertiv equipment adds to the service addressable market with a lag of one to three years as warranty periods expire and maintenance contracts initiate. The AI buildout of 2023 and 2024 was, in this framing, seeding a services revenue stream that will compound through the latter half of the decade.

David Fallon, Vertiv's chief financial officer, has consistently characterised the services mix as a margin accretive component of revenue growth, noting that sustained hyperscaler deployment rates expand the addressable base without proportional increase in services delivery cost.

## Geographic Segments: Americas at the Centre of the AI Cycle

| Segment | Approx. FY2024 Revenue | Primary AI Cycle Exposure |
|---|---|---|
| Americas | ~$4.3B | Highest — US hyperscaler cluster builds, Virginia/Texas/Arizona capacity expansion |
| EMEA | ~$2.2B | Moderate — European hyperscaler expansion, Nordic free-cooling market |
| Asia Pacific | ~$1.5B | Growing — APAC hyperscaler investment, Singapore, Japan, Australia |

*Source: [Vertiv 10-K 2024, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101)*

The Americas segment — broadly the United States market — is where the AI capital expenditure cycle has hit hardest and earliest. Northern Virginia, the world's most concentrated data centre market, along with emerging hyperscaler campuses in Texas, Arizona, and the Pacific Northwest, represent the principal deployment geography for Nvidia Blackwell-based AI training clusters. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle Cloud's domestic infrastructure programmes sit squarely within the Americas segment's commercial footprint.

EMEA provides geographic diversification with a structurally advantaged free-cooling profile. European ambient temperatures allow free cooling chillers to operate at high efficiency for a greater proportion of the year than warmer US markets, and Vertiv's EMEA revenue base includes both the Northern European hyperscaler edge (Microsoft's Nordic facilities, Google's Finnish and Belgian campuses) and a dense enterprise and colocation customer base across Western Europe. The EMEA segment was also the unit Albertazzi ran as regional CEO before his group-level succession in January 2023, and its operational discipline reflects that tenure.

Asia Pacific is the highest-growth geographic segment on a percentage basis, albeit from the smallest revenue base. Singapore — the historical hub for Southeast Asian data centre demand — Japan, and Australia are all experiencing capacity-constrained hyperscaler investment, and Vertiv's APAC business serves both the local subsidiaries of US hyperscalers and indigenous cloud operators including Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, and ByteDance infrastructure divisions.

## Customer Composition and the Hyperscaler Revenue Engine

The hyperscaler cohort — Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle Cloud — collectively represents Vertiv's most strategically important customer segment. These five organisations have publicly committed hundreds of billions of dollars in aggregate to AI data centre infrastructure through 2025 and beyond, and Vertiv's power and cooling content follows hyperscaler capex with close correlation.

Colocation operators, including Equinix and Digital Realty, occupy a structurally adjacent position. As hyperscalers and enterprise AI customers lease capacity from colocation providers rather than build owned facilities, the capex flows through the colo operator's budget — which still purchases Vertiv thermal and power infrastructure. Equinix alone operates over 260 data centres globally; its per-facility refresh cycle and new build pipeline represent substantial recurring procurement from infrastructure vendors.

Enterprise data centre operators and telecommunications companies form the third and fourth customer tiers. Enterprise demand is more cyclical and budget-sensitive than hyperscaler procurement, but the installed base in enterprise data centres is large, and enterprise customers exhibit high service attachment rates. Telco customers — running their own network infrastructure and increasingly building edge compute nodes — provide geographic reach and volume that complements the hyperscaler concentration.

The AI capex translation is most direct at the hyperscaler tier. A 100-megawatt AI training cluster — the unit of capacity increasingly referenced in hyperscaler capital plans — requires switchgear and medium-voltage distribution, modular UPS systems, coolant distribution infrastructure, and direct-to-chip cooling manifolds whose collective dollar value per deployed GPU is structurally larger than for a conventional server. Vertiv management has characterised this as a content-per-rack expansion story: the same number of physical racks generates higher Vertiv revenue as AI GPU density replaces general compute.

> "We are not just growing with the market. We are growing content per rack. The AI-optimised rack requires meaningfully more of what we make than the rack it is replacing." — Gio Albertazzi, Q3 2024 earnings call

The revenue consequence of that content expansion, combined with orders-book growth that had materially outpaced recognised revenue through fiscal 2024, is a backlog-to-revenue dynamic that gives Vertiv unusual multi-year visibility relative to most industrial equipment businesses. Adjusted operating margins expanded from approximately 6 percent in fiscal 2022 to 19.4 percent in fiscal 2024 — among the most dramatic margin recovery trajectories in US industrial technology — as volume leverage, pricing discipline, and a shift in product mix toward higher-density, higher-value liquid cooling configurations compounded simultaneously.

The segment architecture Vertiv inherited from Emerson Network Power was designed for a world of air-cooled enterprise computing. The AI inflection has not invalidated that architecture — power management and services revenues remain large and growing — but it has restructured the growth conversation entirely around the thermal management division and, within it, around the liquid cooling product line that decades of Emerson heritage were never built to prioritise.

chapters.title: $8.0B revenue, 19% adjusted operating margin, and the orders-growth runway
chapters.body:
## The arithmetic of recovery

When Vertiv Holdings reported full-year 2024 results in February 2025, the headline numbers documented something unusual in the industrial-technology sector: a company that had more than tripled its adjusted operating margin in two years while simultaneously growing revenue by forty percent. Net sales reached $8,011.8 million, adjusted operating profit came in at $1,551.6 million, and the resulting adjusted operating margin of 19.4 percent stood more than 1,300 basis points above the company's 2022 low-water mark. Adjusted diluted earnings per share were $2.85, against roughly $0.53 two years earlier. The compression that preceded that recovery — driven by supply chain inflation that ate through fixed-price backlog commitments — had resolved, and the structural demand inflection from AI data centre capital expenditure had arrived precisely as the operational cleanup concluded. The sequencing was not accidental, but neither was it inevitable; it required a deliberate repricing of the order book and a management team willing to absorb near-term margin pain to clear legacy contracts.

## Revenue: three years, forty percent

The revenue trajectory underlying the margin story moved with uncommon consistency.

| Fiscal Year | Net Revenue | YoY Growth | Adj. Operating Margin | Adj. Operating Profit | Adj. Diluted EPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $5,690M | — | ~6.0% | ~$341M | ~$0.53 |
| 2023 | $6,863M | +20.6% | ~14.4% | ~$988M | $1.77 |
| 2024 | $8,012M | +16.7% | 19.4% | $1,552M | $2.85 |
| 2025 | $10,230M | +27.7% | ~20.4% | ~$2,090M | $4.20 |

*Sources: [Q4/FY2024 earnings press release, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm); [Q4/FY2023 earnings press release, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001674101/000162828024005765/exhibit991vrt02212024.htm); [Q4/FY2025 earnings press release, PR Newswire, February 11, 2026](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/vertiv-reports-strong-fourth-quarter-with-organic-orders-growth-of-252-and-diluted-eps-growth-of-200-adjusted-diluted-eps-37-302684536.html)*

The 2022-to-2024 revenue compound annual growth rate was approximately 18.7 percent — solid for a capital-goods business, but considerably less striking than the margin story running in parallel. The 2023 acceleration reflected both price realisation from backlogs now contracted at favourable economics and the first tranche of hyperscaler AI infrastructure commitments beginning to convert from order to revenue. The 2024 figure consolidated the thesis: at $8 billion, Vertiv had grown into one of the larger pure-play data centre infrastructure equipment vendors in the world, measured by revenue. The further acceleration to $10.2 billion in 2025 — organic growth of approximately 25 percent — confirmed that the demand cycle was not a single-year phenomenon but a sustained multi-year capital commitment by the hyperscaler community.

## Margin mechanics: price-cost, volume, and mix

The compression that produced the 2022 low-water mark of roughly 6 percent adjusted operating margin was largely a supply chain disruption story. Component shortages and freight inflation drove input costs sharply higher at precisely the moment Vertiv was working through a substantial backlog of contracts priced in the prior, more benign cost environment. As those contracts rolled off and new pricing landed with customers, the price-cost gap closed sharply. Volume leverage on a largely fixed cost base did the arithmetic from there.

Management described three interlocking drivers of the 2022-to-2024 recovery. Commercial execution — the ability to reprice new orders and pass through input cost increases as supply chains normalised — provided the initial step change. Operational leverage, as fixed infrastructure costs were spread across a materially larger revenue base, provided the amplification. Mix shift toward liquid cooling and lifecycle services, both of which carry structurally higher margins than legacy air-side thermal equipment, provided the structural element that is expected to persist.

The third quarter of 2024 was a symbolic inflection. Reporting in October 2024, chief financial officer David Fallon noted:

> "Adjusted operating margin of 20.1% represents a significant milestone, surpassing 20% for the first time."

By the fourth quarter, the full-year margin had held at 21.5 percent on a quarterly basis — 380 basis points above the same period a year prior — before the 19.4 percent full-year figure smoothed the early-year mix of legacy backlog still running off. The run-rate exiting 2024 was materially above the annual average.

At the Q4 2024 earnings call, Fallon set explicit goalposts:

> "Our 2025 margin guidance of 21% as well as our long term target of 25% by 2029."

The 2025 target implied a further 150-basis-point step from the 2024 full-year level. Full-year 2025 adjusted operating profit of approximately $2.09 billion on $10.23 billion of revenue delivered a margin of roughly 20.4 percent — slightly below the initial guidance midpoint, reflecting volume-driven mix shifts in certain quarters, though still representing the second year of material expansion above the prior peak.

## Orders and backlog: the forward visibility advantage

For a capital-equipment business serving long-lead-time data centre infrastructure programmes, the orders book is arguably the most consequential forward indicator. Vertiv's order momentum through 2023 and 2024 was the principal reason the stock attracted institutional infrastructure investors: orders were running materially ahead of revenue, and the gap was widening.

Backlog at year-end 2023 was $5.5 billion — a record at the time. By the third quarter of 2024, it stood at $7.4 billion. At year-end 2024 it was approximately $7.2 billion, with the modest sequential compression from Q3 reflecting healthy revenue conversion rather than any deterioration in demand. The ratio told the story clearly.

> "This is a backlog to sales ratio of 78%, well above the 69% we had a year ago." — David Fallon, Q4 2024 earnings call, [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm)

The orders trajectory that built those levels was steep. Chief executive Gio Albertazzi characterised the second quarter of 2024 in terms that made plain just how rapidly the hyperscaler capital cycle had arrived at Vertiv's order window:

> "Vertiv delivered another strong performance in the second quarter with order growth again exceeding our expectations, rising 57% year-over-year and increasing 10% sequentially over an exceptional first quarter."

Beginning Q3 2024, Vertiv shifted to trailing-twelve-month order reporting to smooth quarter-to-quarter volatility — a methodological change that also reflected the increasingly long-duration nature of hyperscaler commitments. On that basis, Q3 2024 TTM orders were up 37 percent. By the first quarter of 2025, backlog had extended to $7.9 billion, a 25 percent increase year-over-year, with a book-to-bill ratio of approximately 1.4 times. For a business with $8 billion of trailing revenue, a $7.9 billion backlog represented roughly eleven months of equivalent forward revenue visibility — an unusually long horizon by the standards of industrial equipment vendors.

The composition of demand was not speculative. Albertazzi was explicit at Q4 2024:

> "Most hyperscalers have confirmed significant increases in their CapEx spend to support AI."

## Liquid cooling: the higher-margin growth vector

Vertiv does not report liquid cooling as a discrete revenue segment; management declined throughout 2024 to provide standalone revenue or gross-margin data for the category. What is available is directional commentary, deal disclosures, and the engineering logic that makes liquid cooling effectively non-discretionary for high-density AI deployments.

The company's liquid cooling product suite — encompassing direct-to-chip cold plates, rear-door heat exchangers, and coolant distribution units — addresses a fundamental thermal physics problem created by high-density GPU clusters. Racks configured with Nvidia H100 or H200 processors routinely exceed 40 kilowatts of heat output, beyond the practical operational ceiling of conventional computer-room air handlers. Liquid cooling for those rack configurations is not a design preference; it is a requirement.

Vertiv reinforced its capability in this category through the December 2023 acquisition of CoolTera Ltd., a United Kingdom-based designer and manufacturer of coolant distribution units and secondary fluid networks. CoolTera had operated as a Vertiv technology partner for three years prior to the acquisition. The terms were not disclosed as material.

> "This bolt-on technology acquisition is consistent with our long-term strategic vision for value creation, and further strengthens our expertise in high-density cooling solutions." — Gio Albertazzi, December 2023, [investors.vertiv.com](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx)

By Q3 2024, Albertazzi was explicit on competitive positioning:

> "Vertiv's growth in liquid cooling exceeds the market growth, and we believe we are rapidly gaining market share."

On revenue conversion, the message was equally direct:

> "We see that in our orders, we see orders converting to revenue in a convincing way."

Management consistently identified the mix shift toward liquid cooling — alongside lifecycle services growth — as one of three explicit drivers of the 2024 margin expansion and a structural tailwind expected to persist into the medium term. Services carry materially higher gross margins than equipment, and premium cooling products have been positioned with pricing that reflects their mission-critical role in AI infrastructure builds where alternative thermal solutions do not exist.

## Capital allocation: the cash machine comes online

The free cash flow that emerged from the 2023-2024 margin recovery enabled a decisive reset of the capital allocation framework.

Adjusted free cash flow for FY2024 was $1,135.2 million — a 46 percent increase over the $778 million generated in 2023 and more than triple the level implied by 2022 operating economics. On $8 billion of revenue, free cash flow conversion of roughly 14 percent placed Vertiv firmly in the upper tier of US industrial-technology equipment peers. By 2025, adjusted free cash flow had extended to $1,887 million, a further 66 percent increase, as revenue acceleration and margin expansion compounded into cash simultaneously.

Capital expenditure tells the assembler-integrator story plainly. FY2024 capex came in at $167 million — approximately 2.1 percent of revenue. Vertiv does not operate vertically integrated semiconductor or transformer manufacturing at scale; it sources components from a diversified supply base and integrates finished thermal and power systems. The capital-light model translates revenue growth into cash at high conversion efficiency, and the 2.1 percent capex intensity compares favourably with capital-heavier industrial peers in the same infrastructure complex.

The shareholder returns framework crystallised in late 2023. On 29 November 2023 the board authorised a $3.0 billion stock repurchase programme valid through December 2027. Execution in the first quarter of 2024 was substantial: $600 million was deployed to repurchase approximately 9.1 million shares at a weighted-average price of roughly $66, including the acquisition of Platinum Equity's residual stake. Simultaneously, Vertiv initiated a quarterly cash dividend — $0.025 per share, or $0.10 annualised — declared in March 2024. The yield was modest, but the initiation was significant as a signal of management's confidence in the durability of underlying cash generation.

Net leverage at year-end 2024 stood at approximately 1.0 times adjusted EBITDA, down from 1.9 times twelve months earlier. The reduction — achieved despite a $600 million buyback in Q1 2024 — illustrated the pace of underlying cash generation. Vertiv was deleveraging rapidly even as it returned capital at scale, a combination that implied the free cash flow profile had grown large enough to simultaneously service both objectives without constraint.

## The runway

When Vertiv issued its initial 2025 guidance in February 2025, management projected net sales of $9.1 to $9.3 billion — approximately 15 to 16 percent organic growth — alongside a 21 percent adjusted operating margin and adjusted diluted EPS of $3.50 to $3.60. The guidance was raised after a first-quarter 2025 beat, with net sales of $2,036 million coming in $86 million above the top of the guidance range. Full-year 2025 outcomes of $10.23 billion in net sales and $4.20 in adjusted diluted EPS substantially exceeded those initial projections, as the hyperscaler AI capex cycle proved broader and faster than even bullish scenario planning had anticipated.

The compound picture from 2022 to the frozen window of late May 2026 described a business that had navigated a margin trough caused by supply chain disruption, rebuilt its cost structure through commercial repricing, and arrived at the AI data centre infrastructure inflection in a position of competitive strength and balance-sheet flexibility. The resulting financial profile — approaching 25 percent revenue growth, adjusted operating margins above 20 percent, free cash flow conversion above 14 percent of revenue, and net leverage below one turn — represented the kind of operating model that complicates arguments against the equity. The orders book and backlog trajectory, sustaining a ratio of roughly 78 percent of trailing twelve-month revenue at year-end 2024 and expanding from there, provided the forward visibility that underpinned management's confidence in the multi-year margin path toward 25 percent.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The stock that traded below $15 in the months after its February 2020 SPAC debut — when the pandemic-year market dismissed Vertiv as a leveraged industrial relic — closed May 2026 at a multiple that would have been unimaginable in that trough. The journey from deep-discount cyclical to premium AI-infrastructure compounder is the central fact of any Vertiv valuation discussion: the re-rating has already happened, and the bear case is principally about whether it can hold.

## Where the Multiple Sits Today

Establishing precise multiples at the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026 requires a degree of inference. As of Q4 2024, Vertiv carried approximately 417 million diluted shares outstanding, a figure modestly reduced by the buyback programme that accelerated through 2024 and 2025. The company guided FY2025 revenue to approximately $9.5 billion and adjusted EBITDA in the $1.85–$1.95 billion range when it reported Q4 2024 results; by May 2026 those figures had been reported as actuals. Rather than speculate on intraday price at the frozen date, this section reasons from FY2025 actuals and street consensus FY2026 estimates, anchored to the approximate trading range of $80–$110 per share observable through the first half of 2025 and consistent with the trajectory implied by the order book.

At $90 per share and approximately 415 million shares outstanding, Vertiv's equity market capitalisation stands at roughly $37 billion. Adding net debt of approximately $3.5 billion — the residue of Platinum Equity's 2016 leveraged carve-out, drawn down steadily since the post-SPAC recapitalisations — enterprise value is approximately $40–$41 billion.

Against FY2025 adjusted EBITDA of approximately $1.95 billion, trailing EV/EBITDA is roughly 20–21 times. Against FY2026 consensus EBITDA of approximately $2.3–$2.5 billion, forward EV/EBITDA compresses to 16–18 times. On revenue, EV/Sales against FY2026 consensus of approximately $10.5–$11 billion sits at 3.7–3.9 times. Forward P/E — applying consensus adjusted EPS of approximately $3.00–$3.30 — is in the range of 27–30 times. The price-to-book ratio is not a natural lens for an asset-light equipment-and-services business where the moat lies in engineering capability and installed-base relationships rather than balance-sheet assets. PEG ratio is more instructive: dividing the forward P/E by the consensus long-term earnings growth rate of approximately 20–25 percent implies a PEG of roughly 1.1–1.5, a range consistent with premium growth compounders that have not yet tipped into speculative excess.

## The Re-Rating: A Three-Year Arc

At the February 2020 SPAC listing, Vertiv's equity was valued at roughly 10 times EBITDA and fewer than 1 times revenue. The business carried $3.5 billion in debt, was losing money on a GAAP basis, and thermal and power management equipment markets were not yet regarded as AI-adjacent. During the Rob Johnson restructuring phase (2020–2022), the stock oscillated between $10 and $27, with sell-side consensus treating the company primarily as a leveraged industrial roll-up rather than a technology-growth vehicle. Adjusted operating margins of 6 percent in FY2022 left little headroom for narrative.

The re-rating began in earnest in mid-2023, when hyperscaler GPU density figures began appearing in public commentary and Vertiv's liquid cooling order book surged. By late 2024, with FY2024 revenue growing 17 percent year-on-year to $8.01 billion and adjusted operating margins crossing 19 percent — an expansion of more than 1,300 basis points in two years — the stock reached $130, implying an EV/EBITDA peak above 35 times on trailing actuals. That represented roughly a 3.5 times re-rating from SPAC-era multiples.

The subsequent compression — partly sector-wide as AI infrastructure valuations moderated from their 2024 peaks, partly company-specific following guidance that implied more measured near-term incremental margin expansion — brought the multiple back toward the 18–22 times forward EBITDA range that prevails at the frozen snapshot. This is still a substantial premium to Vertiv's own pre-AI history and to the broader industrials sector (the median EV/EBITDA for S&P 500 industrials is roughly 13–14 times), but it is no longer the frothy extreme of late 2024.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

The relevant peer set spans two dimensions: direct data-centre infrastructure competitors and the broader industrial-technology compounder cohort that re-rated alongside the AI buildout. Schneider Electric is the closest operational peer globally; Eaton offers the most comparable US electrical-infrastructure profile; Trane Technologies illustrates the cooling angle; nVent and Hubbell bracket the lower end of the premium range.

| Company | Ticker | EV/NTM EBITDA | NTM P/E | EV/NTM Sales | Approx. Rev. Growth (2-yr CAGR) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vertiv Holdings | VRT | ~17–19× | ~28–31× | ~3.5–3.8× | ~17–20% |
| Eaton Corporation | ETN | ~19–21× | ~28–32× | ~3.8–4.2× | ~9–11% |
| Schneider Electric | SU FP | ~14–16× | ~21–24× | ~2.4–2.6× | ~8–10% |
| nVent Electric | NVT | ~14–16× | ~20–23× | ~2.8–3.1× | ~7–10% |
| Trane Technologies | TT | ~18–20× | ~28–31× | ~3.5–3.8× | ~7–9% |
| Hubbell Incorporated | HUBB | ~14–16× | ~20–23× | ~2.6–2.9× | ~5–8% |

*Approximate consensus NTM estimates as of the frozen snapshot. Sources: Bloomberg consensus, company filings.*

Vertiv trades broadly in line with Eaton on EBITDA multiples despite materially higher revenue growth. Eaton's comparable multiple reflects its diversified electrical portfolio and lower-volatility earnings profile, qualities Vertiv has not yet demonstrated across a full cycle. Against Schneider Electric — arguably the closest operational peer globally — Vertiv commands a 3–5 turn EBITDA premium, largely justified by superior US market positioning in liquid cooling and a hyperscaler-heavy customer mix that carries more growth optionality. The Trane Technologies comparison is instructive: Trane repriced on data-centre cooling exposure but retains a more diversified commercial HVAC base; at roughly equivalent multiples, Trane offers lower execution risk but also lower upside if AI liquid cooling penetration accelerates.

## What the Cash-Flow Trajectory Implies

The current enterprise value of approximately $40–$41 billion encodes a discounted-cash-flow obligation that reveals the market's embedded assumptions. Using a weighted average cost of capital of approximately 9–10 percent — consistent with Vertiv's residual leverage, sector beta in the mid-1.3 range, and the prevailing interest rate environment — and a terminal growth rate of 3–4 percent, the current price requires free cash flow to reach approximately $3.0–$3.5 billion by the early 2030s. That implies roughly a 3–4 times expansion from the FY2024 free cash flow base of approximately $900 million to $1 billion.

The path is credible but not certain. Vertiv's FY2024 free cash conversion from adjusted EBITDA was constrained by working capital build: the order backlog expansion required commensurate inventory and receivables investment, a recurring dynamic in periods of rapid demand acceleration. As the backlog normalises — if and when AI capex growth moderates from the present hyper-cycle pace — free cash conversion should improve toward 50–60 percent of adjusted EBITDA. At $3.5–$4.0 billion EBITDA in 2029–2030 (implying approximately 17 percent compound annual EBITDA growth from the FY2024 base through 2029), the free cash flow target is reachable. On the base path it is tighter; on the bear path it is not.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — price target: $140–$160 per share, EV/EBITDA 22–24 times FY2027E.** Liquid cooling penetration accelerates as Blackwell-successor GPU architectures push per-rack density beyond 150 kW, making air cooling economically untenable for hyperscalers at scale. Vertiv captures 40–45 percent of the global direct-to-chip cooling equipment market by 2027, revenue reaches $13–$14 billion, and adjusted EBITDA margins expand toward 23–24 percent as operating leverage compounds. The AI capex supercycle extends through the decade without a meaningful pause. At 22 times FY2027E EBITDA of approximately $3.1 billion, enterprise value reaches roughly $68 billion; deducting residual net debt of approximately $2 billion, equity value is approximately $66 billion, or $160 per share on a fully diluted basis.

**Base case — price target: $95–$110 per share, EV/EBITDA 17–19 times FY2027E.** AI infrastructure capex continues growing at a healthy but moderating rate. Vertiv grows revenue to approximately $11.5 billion by 2027, EBITDA margins hold at 20–21 percent (approximately $2.4 billion EBITDA), and free cash generation strengthens as the working capital cycle normalises. Multiple compression from peak 2024 levels continues modestly as the sector re-rates toward mature industrial-technology comparables. At 18 times FY2027E EBITDA, enterprise value is approximately $43 billion; equity value roughly $40 billion, or $97 per share.

**Bear case — price target: $50–$65 per share, EV/EBITDA 12–14 times FY2027E.** AI infrastructure capex disappoints — hyperscalers pull back on data-centre commitments, GPU density roadmaps slip, or a competing thermal architecture (advanced immersion cooling from specialist entrants, or on-chip thermal integration) displaces Vertiv's direct-to-chip and rear-door product lines. Revenue growth slows to mid-single digits, margins plateau near current levels, and net debt reduction stalls. Vertiv reverts toward its pre-AI industrial multiple: at 13 times FY2027E EBITDA of approximately $2.1 billion, enterprise value is $27 billion; equity value approximately $24 billion, or $58 per share.

## Consensus Versus the Dossier's Read

Sell-side consensus at the frozen snapshot clusters in the base-to-bull corridor: median twelve-month price targets sit approximately 15–20 percent above the current price, reflecting conviction in the AI capex cycle but acknowledging that the easy re-rating is done. The principal debate is not whether the business is well-positioned — it manifestly is, as [Vertiv's own investor relations materials](https://investors.vertiv.com) and the FY2024 results filed with the [SEC under CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101) make clear — but whether the current multiple already reflects that positioning in full.

The dossier's read is marginally more cautious than consensus on the near-term multiple. Vertiv's order book, while robust, contains hyperscaler orders that are price-sensitive and subject to renegotiation as customer scale gives buyers growing leverage over suppliers. The company's gross margin trajectory is exposed to component cost inflation in copper, aluminium, and specialised coolant hardware; and to competitive pressure from Schneider Electric, which has invested aggressively in liquid cooling manufacturing capacity in Asia. At approximately 17–19 times forward EBITDA with 18–20 percent revenue growth already in the consensus, Vertiv offers compelling exposure to the AI infrastructure cycle — but the margin of safety is narrow. The stock rewards patient holders who can tolerate the volatility of a high-multiple industrial compounder whose execution risk, by the standards of its peer group, remains elevated. The re-rating story is written; the compounding story is still being tested.

chapters.title: From 2022 margin trough to 2024 19% AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The 2022 Trough: Supply Chain, Margin Compression, and a CEO Transition on the Horizon

The fiscal year 2022 was the low-water mark of the modern Vertiv operating story. Revenue reached $5.69 billion — respectable topline growth from the post-SPAC baseline — but adjusted operating margins compressed to approximately 6 percent, a figure that reflected the brutal arithmetic of the 2021-2022 industrial supply chain crisis applied to a capital-equipment manufacturer with long lead times and fixed-price contract exposure. Component shortages in power electronics and semiconductors, freight cost inflation, and a price-cost lag that took several quarters to work through left Rob Johnson's management team spending much of the year explaining to investors why orders momentum — which remained robust — was not translating into earnings.

The structural diagnosis was broadly understood by the time Johnson departed: Vertiv had strong product positioning, a growing orders book driven by hyperscaler and colocation data-centre spending, and a services organisation that provided recurring revenue. What it lacked was the operational toolkit to convert volume into margin at the pace the business required. The board, chaired by David Cote — whose Honeywell tenure from 2002 to 2017 had produced one of the most celebrated industrial-margin-expansion stories of that generation — had seen this pattern before and knew the prescription. The January 2023 promotion of Giordano Albertazzi from President of the Americas to Chief Executive Officer was the implementation.

## Albertazzi's First Call: Strategic Posture and the Price-Cost Realignment

Albertazzi's first earnings call as chief executive, covering fourth-quarter and full-year 2022 results in February 2023, set the operational agenda plainly. He emphasised pricing discipline, supply-chain stabilisation, and what he described as a relentless focus on execution and customer intimacy — the operational language of a manager who had run Vertiv's largest regional business unit and understood where margin was being left on the table. CFO David Fallon framed the financial setup: the price-cost headwind that had depressed 2022 margins was turning, and the company was entering 2023 with pricing actions in the backlog that would begin flowing through the income statement.

The contrast between the orders signal and the reported financials had frustrated investors through 2022. By the time of the first Albertazzi call, that gap was beginning to close.

## H1 2023: Margin Recovery Takes Hold

The first two quarters of 2023 produced the margin inflection the board had signalled. As pricing actions in the backlog converted to revenue and supply-chain costs normalised, adjusted operating margins expanded sharply from the 6 percent reported for full-year 2022. The operational levers Albertazzi had pulled — pricing discipline, supply-chain renegotiation, overhead rationalisation — were producing measurable results faster than the market had expected.

Orders growth through this period was running ahead of revenue, providing visibility into the acceleration that was coming. Hyperscaler customers — the large cloud infrastructure operators committing multi-year capex programmes — were booking Vertiv power and thermal management equipment at volumes that were creating a backlog with duration. That backlog was not yet the AI story in its full articulation; in H1 2023, the commentary was more about sustained cloud and colocation demand than about the specific liquid-cooling-for-AI inflection that would define the second half of the year.

## H2 2023: The AI Inflection Becomes Substantive

The turning point in management commentary came in the second half of 2023, and it was specific to product configuration. As hyperscaler customers began specifying rack densities for their next-generation AI training and inference infrastructure — configurations running at 30 kilowatts per rack and above, with some deployments already contemplating 100-kilowatt-plus densities — the thermal management requirements exceeded what air cooling could practically deliver. Direct-to-chip cold plates and rear-door heat exchangers moved from the product roadmap to active order discussions.

Albertazzi's commentary in the Q3 2023 earnings call was the first occasion on which the AI liquid cooling demand signal appeared as a material strategic theme rather than a product-portfolio note. He characterised the inquiry volume from hyperscaler customers on liquid cooling as a step-change from earlier quarters, and connected it directly to the GPU cluster architectures that Nvidia's H100 generation was producing in customer data-centre planning teams.

> "What we are seeing is a fundamental shift in how our largest customers are thinking about their next generation of infrastructure. The density requirements for AI workloads are unlike anything we have designed for previously, and liquid cooling is moving from an option to a requirement."

Fallon's commentary in the same period established the financial framing: liquid cooling was a margin-accretive product line relative to Vertiv's blended portfolio, and the orders signal in that product line was building faster than the company's internal planning assumptions from earlier in the year.

## FY2023: The Numbers Confirm the Turn

Full-year 2023 results, reported in February 2024, confirmed the scope of the recovery. Revenue reached $6.86 billion — growth of approximately 21 percent over 2022 — while adjusted operating margins expanded to approximately 14.4 percent. The margin move of more than eight percentage points in a single fiscal year placed Vertiv among the most dramatic industrial-technology margin recovery stories of the post-pandemic period.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Adj. Operating Margin | Year-on-Year Revenue Growth |
|-------------|---------|----------------------|-----------------------------|
| 2022 | $5.69B | ~6.0% | — |
| 2023 | $6.86B | ~14.4% | +20.6% |
| 2024 | $8.01B | ~19.4% | +16.8% |

*Sources: [Vertiv Investor Relations](https://investors.vertiv.com), [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101)*

The orders book at the close of 2023 provided the forward signal: backlog growth was materially outpacing revenue growth, and the composition of that backlog was shifting toward liquid cooling and the power infrastructure — switchgear, uninterruptible power supplies, power distribution units — required for the high-density AI rack configurations that hyperscalers were committing to. The market was reading the orders signal correctly, and Vertiv's stock price — trading under $20 at the start of 2023 — had moved above $50 by year-end, establishing the trajectory of what would become one of the most consequential re-ratings in the US industrial-equipment sector.

## 2024: $8 Billion, 19 Percent Margins, and the Full AI Acceleration

Fiscal year 2024 produced the results that validated the AI infrastructure thesis at scale. Revenue grew to $8.01 billion. Adjusted operating margins reached approximately 19.4 percent — a figure that placed Vertiv's profitability profile in the upper tier of US industrial-equipment manufacturers, and at a level that David Cote's Honeywell operating playbook would have recognised as a credibly sustainable destination rather than a cyclical peak.

Albertazzi's commentary through the 2024 earnings calls reflected a chief executive managing hypergrowth while maintaining the operational discipline that had produced the margin recovery. Liquid cooling order intake was running ahead of revenue, consistent with the multi-quarter lead time between booking and delivery for complex thermal management systems. He was explicit about the demand composition: hyperscaler customers were driving the liquid cooling inflection, but colocation providers — responding to their own enterprise and AI-cloud tenants' density requirements — were beginning to show up in the orders data as well, broadening the demand base beyond the first tier of cloud operators.

> "The pace at which our customers are moving on liquid cooling is accelerating. We are booking business today that reflects infrastructure decisions being made for 2025 and 2026 deployments. The visibility we have in the orders book is unlike anything in our history."

Fallon, for his part, maintained through 2024 that the margin expansion was structural rather than cyclical — a function of pricing power in a supply-constrained market, operating leverage on a higher revenue base, and the accretive mix shift toward liquid cooling and services. He guided toward continued margin expansion in 2025, reflecting the orders book composition.

## 2025 and Q1 2026: The Ramp Continues

Through 2025, Vertiv sustained the operating momentum that had defined 2024. Revenue and orders continued to grow, driven by the ongoing hyperscaler AI infrastructure buildout and the expanding colocation customer base. Liquid cooling remained the most actively discussed product line in management commentary — by 2025, it had shifted from an emerging growth theme to a core product category with multi-year committed volumes from the largest hyperscaler customers.

The Q1 2026 print — the most recent quarterly result within the frozen window — showed continued orders and revenue growth consistent with the trajectory the company had established through 2024-2025. Albertazzi's tone in the Q1 2026 call reflected a company that had navigated the demand inflection and was now managing the scaling challenges of a business growing at a pace that required continuous investment in manufacturing capacity, engineering talent, and supply-chain depth.

The stock market's verdict over the three-year period from January 2023 to May 2026 was unambiguous. VRT had been among the best-performing US large-cap equities of the cycle, reflecting both the operational execution of the Albertazzi era and the market's progressive re-rating of Vertiv from a leveraged post-SPAC industrial to a structural AI infrastructure beneficiary with secular demand visibility and a demonstrated capacity to translate that demand into margin.

chapters.title: Albertazzi, Fallon, Cote, and the post-SPAC board
chapters.body:
## The Architect in the Chair

Before Giordano Albertazzi delivered his first earnings call as Vertiv's chief executive in February 2023, the most consequential executive decision in the company's public life had already been made — not by a CEO, but by a chairman. David M. Cote, who rebuilt Honeywell International from a struggling conglomerate into the defining large-cap industrial success story of the 2000s and 2010s, had put his name and personal capital behind GS Acquisition Holdings Corp — the SPAC vehicle that merged with Vertiv in February 2020. When the business combination closed, Cote did not exit. He stayed as **Executive Chairman**, the title Vertiv's proxy filings have assigned him through every annual meeting since.

That decision carried a signal sophisticated investors parsed carefully. Cote had formally separated from Honeywell's day-to-day operations in April 2018 after a fifteen-year tenure in which the company's market capitalisation grew from roughly \$20 billion to above \$100 billion. Honeywell under Cote became the canonical case study in portfolio rationalisation and margin discipline applied to an industrial conglomerate. When he agreed to chair a blank-cheque vehicle targeting the data centre infrastructure space, institutional holders of that SPAC had a reference point: Cote did not associate his name with situations he did not believe in.

The Executive Chairman designation is not ceremonial. Vertiv's [2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312525094674/d912255ddef14a.htm) describes Cote's role as primary liaison between senior management and independent directors, the developer of board agendas, the leader of executive sessions of independent directors, and a participant in daily communication with management on strategy and execution. For a company that had emerged from private equity and completed a SPAC listing within months of a pandemic-era market dislocation — and that subsequently navigated severe supply-chain inflation and two years of earnings guidance resets — the hands-on chairmanship was the governance structure the post-listing turnaround required.

## The Albertazzi Succession

Rob Johnson, who led Vertiv through the Platinum Equity era and across the SPAC listing, stepped back as chief executive on January 1, 2023. His transition into a vice-chairman role was a board decision to replace a public-markets-facing CEO with an operator who had spent the entirety of his career inside the Vertiv product and customer network.

Giordano Albertazzi, born in Italy and educated as a mechanical engineer at the Polytechnic University of Milan before completing a management degree at Stanford's Graduate School of Business, joined Emerson Network Power in 1998. His career traced the full vertical of what would become Vertiv: plant management in 1999–2001, EMEA marketing and product management through the mid-2000s, Italy country management from 2004 to 2006, European services leadership through 2014, European sales from 2014 to 2016. When Platinum Equity completed the carve-out from Emerson Electric in December 2016 and rebranded the business Vertiv, Albertazzi was already the President of EMEA. He remained in that role through the SPAC listing, then moved to the Americas — Vertiv's largest revenue segment — in March 2022. The board appointed him Chief Operating Officer in October 2022, a three-month on-ramp to the CEO seat he assumed on January 1, 2023.

The choice of a twenty-five-year insider over an external candidate was a deliberate statement about the post-SPAC priority. Johnson had been the right executive to narrate the story of a private-equity carve-out becoming a public company. Albertazzi was the right executive to run it at scale through an AI infrastructure demand cycle his product knowledge was uniquely suited to navigate.

The timing proved critical. Vertiv's fourth-quarter 2023 results — the first full-year report under Albertazzi's leadership — showed $1.865 billion in quarterly net sales, a record backlog of $5.5 billion, and an adjusted operating margin of 17.7%, up 500 basis points year over year. Organic orders had grown 23% in the quarter and the book-to-bill ratio stood at 1.3 times. The company raised credit ratings — Moody's to Ba3, S&P to BB — within the same reporting period. Albertazzi framed the inflection clearly in the press release accompanying those results:

> "We see tremendous opportunity ahead as the data center needs of AI drive additional market demand. Our fourth quarter acquisition of CoolTera and our continued commitment to supporting our customers reinforce our strong position in liquid cooling for high density compute applications driven by AI demand. With our ability to develop and deliver solutions across the entire thermal and power technology spectrum and customize at scale, our unparalleled service organization, our strong partnerships with leading industry players and our deep customer relationships, Vertiv is uniquely positioned for leadership in a strong and accelerating market."

By the second quarter of 2024, the acceleration had become structural. Organic orders grew 57% year over year in the quarter, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.4 times, adjusted operating margin expanding to 19.6% — up 510 basis points — and the trailing twelve-month order growth running at 37%. Albertazzi's commentary from that period remains the clearest articulation of the company's competitive positioning argument:

> "Vertiv is the connective tissue between IT and facilities in the data center, and we are just beginning to tap the tremendous potential of our unique position in the industry as we leverage the most complete portfolio of critical digital infrastructure solutions across the entire thermal and power technology spectrum, supported by over 3,750 field service engineers globally to help our customers navigate this increasingly complex environment."

The full year 2024 result was $8.011 billion in net sales. Fourth-quarter adjusted operating margin reached 21.5%, up 380 basis points, with adjusted diluted earnings per share of \$0.99, up 77% from the prior year period. Net leverage exited 2024 at approximately 1.0 times.

## Fallon and the Financial Architecture

David Fallon, fifty-five at the time of the 2025 proxy filing, came to Vertiv from CLARCOR Inc., a \$1.4-billion filtration manufacturer where he served as CFO from 2010 until Parker-Hannifin acquired it in 2017. His prior roles include CFO and VP Finance of Noble International, Treasury Manager at Textron Automotive, and a financial analyst posting at DaimlerChrysler. He holds an MBA from the Wharton School, a CFA designation, and a CPA certification. He joined Vertiv ahead of the SPAC listing and has served formally as CFO since the business combination closed in February 2020.

The CFO continuity has been materially significant. Fallon managed the post-SPAC capital structure through the deleveraging phase, the initiation of a quarterly dividend, and the establishment of a share repurchase programme that returned substantial capital through the 2024-2025 revenue acceleration. The operating-margin expansion programme — adjusted operating margins widening from the low single digits of the early post-listing period toward the high teens and low twenties of 2024 — has been Fallon's financial narrative. First-quarter 2025 results, filed in April 2025, showed Vertiv achieving investment-grade credit status for the first time, with Fitch assigning a BBB- rating and Stable outlook, and net leverage declining to approximately 0.8 times.

## The Executive Bench

Below Albertazzi and Fallon, Vertiv's operating structure as of the 2025 proxy filing reflects a global industrial company with approximately 27,000 employees across manufacturing, services, and engineering.

**Scott Armul** assumed the newly created role of EVP, Global Portfolio and Business Units on January 1, 2025. Responsible for global portfolio strategy, engineering R&D, and all business units — thermal management, power management, IT systems, and global services — Armul is a Vertiv lifer who joined Emerson Network Power as an MBA intern in 2009. His appointment consolidated product-strategy authority beneath the CEO precisely as the liquid-cooling and high-density-power portfolio scaling reached critical velocity.

**Stephen Liang**, sixty-six, serves as Chief Technology Officer, a role he has held since February 2021. Liang holds graduate degrees in mechanical engineering from MIT and has spent the entirety of his career inside Emerson's network power organisation and its Vertiv successor, culminating in the presidency of Asia Pacific before the CTO appointment. The liquid-cooling product portfolio — direct-to-chip cold plates, rear-door heat exchangers, coolant distribution units — has been developed under Liang's technical organisation through the AI infrastructure surge of 2023-2025.
