**Anand Sanghi** leads the Americas as regional president, the role Albertazzi vacated on his promotion to COO in late 2022. **Karsten Winther** has led EMEA since March 2022, the region Albertazzi built before his Americas appointment. **Edward Cui** runs Greater China, where Vertiv has maintained local manufacturing and customer relationships across more than two decades. **Anders Karlborg**, EVP for Manufacturing, Logistics and Operational Excellence since August 2023, brings supply-chain leadership from Volvo, Ericsson, Huawei, and ZTE. **Paul Ryan** as Chief Procurement Officer oversees approximately \$4.7 billion in direct and indirect spend across roughly 8,000 suppliers, a function that became strategically central through the supply-chain disruption of 2021-2022 and has remained so as liquid-cooling component sourcing for hyperscaler programmes has scaled.

## Board Composition: The Pedigree Concentration

Vertiv's ten-member board as of the [2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312525094674/d912255ddef14a.htm) — eight independent directors plus Cote and Albertazzi — reflects a composition strategy assembled at the SPAC listing and maintained with two calibrated additions in 2022.

| Director | Background | On Board Since |
|---|---|---|
| David M. Cote (Exec. Chair) | Honeywell Chairman & CEO 2002–2017; GE; TRW | Feb 2020 |
| Giordano Albertazzi | CEO; 25+ years Emerson/Vertiv | Jan 2023 |
| Roger Fradin | Honeywell Vice Chairman; ACS President 2004–2014 | Feb 2020 |
| Edward L. Monser | Emerson President 2010–2018; COO 2001–2015 | Feb 2020 |
| Jacob Kotzubei | Co-President, Platinum Equity | Feb 2020 |
| Matthew Louie | Managing Director, Platinum Equity | Feb 2020 |
| Steven S. Reinemund | PepsiCo Chairman & CEO 2001–2006 | Feb 2020 |
| Joseph van Dokkum | UTC Power; Siemens Power T&D; Kleiner Perkins OP | Feb 2020 |
| Joseph J. DeAngelo | HD Supply CEO; Home Depot EVP; GE career | Oct 2022 |
| Jakki L. Haussler | Opus Capital Management founder; former CPA | Aug 2022 |

The structural feature is the Honeywell-Emerson-Platinum concentration, and it is intentional. Cote and Roger Fradin — who chaired Honeywell's Compensation Committee throughout Cote's tenure and served as Vice Chairman through April 2017 before retiring — between them represent more than fifteen years of Honeywell board-level and CEO-level decision-making. Fradin chairs Vertiv's own Compensation Committee, replicating a governance dynamic Honeywell investors would have recognised. Edward Monser spent three decades inside Emerson Electric's senior operating leadership and was the company's President from 2010 to 2018 — he was the direct Emerson executive counterpart to the Network Power carve-out that created Vertiv, giving the board an institutional memory no post-listing hire could approximate. Jacob Kotzubei and Matthew Louie represent Platinum Equity's two continuing board seats, preserving private-equity operating perspective from the firm that rebuilt the business between 2016 and 2020.

The 2022 additions — Joseph DeAngelo in October, Jakki Haussler in August — expanded the board's operational and financial governance depth. DeAngelo led HD Supply as a standalone public company through its separation from Home Depot, a carve-out-to-independent narrative with structural parallels to Vertiv's own Emerson origin. Haussler, the founder and former CEO of Opus Capital Management and a former certified public accountant, adds financial audit rigour; she sits on the Audit Committee under Steven Reinemund's chairmanship alongside Monser.

The committee structure encodes the board's governance priorities: Reinemund, the PepsiCo CEO, chairs Audit; Fradin, the Honeywell industrialist, chairs Compensation; van Dokkum, whose career spans UTC Power and Siemens Power Transmission and Distribution, chairs Nominating and Corporate Governance. The alignment of Fradin's industrial-equipment operating pedigree with the Compensation Committee — the body setting incentive structure for the management team through the AI infrastructure cycle — is the board's most deliberate governance signal.

The composition argues a legible thesis for investors assessing Vertiv as an AI infrastructure pure-play: this is a company whose governance was assembled for the industrial-equipment market cycle, calibrated for margin discipline, operational turnaround, and the long-cycle purchasing rhythms of hyperscaler and colocation infrastructure procurement. The concentration of Honeywell, Emerson, and Platinum institutional memory at the board table was not incidental to the post-SPAC recovery. It was the mechanism.

---

*Sources: [Vertiv DEF 14A Proxy Statement, filed April 25, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312525094674/d912255ddef14a.htm); [Vertiv Q4 2024 Earnings Release, 8-K filed February 12, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm); [Q3 2024 Earnings Release, 8-K filed October 23, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024043343/q32024exhibit991vrt102324.htm); [Q2 2024 Earnings Release, 8-K filed July 24, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024032675/q22024exhibit991vrt072424.htm); [Q4/FY 2023 Earnings Release, 8-K filed February 21, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024005765/exhibit991vrt02212024.htm); [Q1 2025 Earnings Release, 8-K filed April 23, 2025](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025018915/q12025exhibit991vrt042325.htm); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101).*

chapters.title: Hyperscalers, colocation, enterprise, and the components supply chain
chapters.body:
## A tiered customer architecture

Vertiv's revenue sits at the intersection of every meaningful tier of data centre operator: the hyperscale cloud providers who have turned AI infrastructure into a capital deployment programme of historic scale; the colocation companies who have discovered that the AI buildout is reshaping their whole business; the enterprise organisations still running on-premises infrastructure; and the telecommunications carriers whose edge and backbone nodes require the same critical power and thermal management kit. Each tier matters, but they are not equally important, and the hierarchy has shifted materially since the AI inflection of 2023.

The principal growth engine is cloud and hyperscale. Vertiv's [2024 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101&type=10-K) describes cloud and hyperscale facilities as "massive in scale, can span multiple acres and are primarily used to support cloud applications," adding that this portion of the industry "is growing rapidly." Vertiv does not disclose individual hyperscaler customer names in its SEC filings — in keeping with the non-disclosure framework that governs most of its major contracts — but the aggregate hyperscale and cloud vertical is identified as representing a "material portion" of the customer base and is understood by investors to encompass Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta's infrastructure organisation, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, among others. All five of those operators dramatically accelerated data centre capital expenditure commitments from 2023 onwards as their AI compute programmes demanded GPU cluster infrastructure that air cooling could no longer adequately serve.

The 10-K is explicit about the pricing dynamics this concentration creates: "Large companies, such as communication network and cloud/hyperscale and colocation data center providers, comprise a material portion of our customer base and generally have greater purchasing power than smaller entities. Accordingly, these customers often have enhanced leverage that allow them to require more favorable terms and conditions in their contracts with us." For Vertiv, the trade-off is structural: accepting some margin pressure from the largest accounts in exchange for the volume, backlog visibility, and engineering collaboration that comes with supplying the AI industry's tier-one operators.

## The colocation segment and named customers

Vertiv's 10-K names its colocation customer category explicitly and, unusually for a company of its scale, provides representative examples directly in the body of its annual filing. Among the colocation operators cited are [Digital Realty](https://www.digitalrealty.com/), [Equinix](https://www.equinix.com/), Compass Datacenters, and QTS — a roster that spans the largest publicly traded colocation companies in the United States and several of the most ambitious campus developers targeting hyperscaler anchor tenants.

This matters for Vertiv's growth profile. The annual report notes that the colocation market "is on a significant growth trajectory," with management-level commentary pegging the segment's capacity expansion at 15–17% compound annual rates. Colocation differs from hyperscale in one structurally important respect for an infrastructure equipment supplier: colocation operators procure power and thermal equipment to spec for their own facilities before tenants arrive, and then lease capacity to cloud providers and enterprises that may not themselves have the engineering teams to specify bespoke builds. That positions Vertiv as an upstream vendor to the entire chain — selling equipment to Equinix or Digital Realty whose own customers may include the same hyperscale names that Vertiv also serves directly. The 10-K's Compass Datacenters partnership is an illustration: the two companies co-developed the Vertiv CoolPhase Flex, a first-of-its-kind hybrid system that combines refrigerant-based air cooling and liquid cooling into a single flexible unit, capable of shifting between modalities to accommodate varying rack power densities across the same floor.

Enterprise data centre operators — the 10-K names Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Walmart, and Allianz as representative examples — constitute the third category. Management commentary acknowledges that enterprise data centre square footage "has generally been flat for the past three years," reflecting the broad migration of enterprise IT workloads to public cloud. Enterprise demand for Vertiv's services and replacement equipment, however, remains durable, supported by regulatory requirements around data sovereignty and the persistence of on-premises infrastructure in financial services, healthcare, and manufacturing.

## Americas dominance and geographic exposure

Vertiv segments its business across three geographies — Americas, Asia Pacific, and Europe, Middle East and Africa — and the ordering is deliberate. The Americas produced net sales of $4.50 billion in fiscal year 2024, representing 56 per cent of the company's $8.01 billion consolidated revenue. Asia Pacific contributed $1.72 billion (22 per cent) and EMEA added $1.79 billion (the remaining 22 per cent). The relative proportions were identical in fiscal year 2023, when Americas held the same 56 per cent share — a sign that the AI-driven demand surge has been geographically broad, lifting all three segments, rather than concentrated in any single region.

| Segment | FY2024 Revenue | FY2023 Revenue | YoY Growth | FY2024 Op. Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Americas | $4,500.6M | $3,844.5M | +17.1% | 24.4% |
| Asia Pacific | $1,717.8M | $1,527.8M | +12.4% | 10.2% |
| EMEA | $1,793.4M | $1,490.9M | +20.3% | 24.5% |
| **Total** | **$8,011.8M** | **$6,863.2M** | **+16.7%** | — |

*Source: [Vertiv Holdings Co Form 10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101&type=10-K)*

The margin disparity between regions is striking. Americas and EMEA both operated above 24 per cent in fiscal 2024, while Asia Pacific managed only 10.2 per cent. The compression in APAC partly reflects the product mix: the region skews toward lower-margin power management and thermal products for the communications market, and the competitive environment is more intense, with local Chinese manufacturers — Huawei and a cluster of domestic data centre equipment companies — willing to bid aggressively. The 10-K lists Huawei Investment & Holding Co. as a principal large-scale competitor across all three regions.

The order backlog reveals where demand is accelerating fastest. At December 31, 2024, Vertiv's total backlog stood at $7.18 billion, up $1.65 billion or 29.9 per cent from $5.53 billion twelve months earlier. The Americas segment accounted for $4.67 billion of that total — up 38.8 per cent year on year — reflecting the dominant share of US hyperscaler and colocation capex in the global AI buildout. Asia Pacific backlog grew 47.8 per cent to $911 million, the fastest proportional rate, as the region begins to absorb its own AI infrastructure wave. EMEA backlog rose only 3.2 per cent to $1.60 billion, suggesting a lag in European AI capital deployment relative to North America, though the region's high revenue-to-backlog conversion rate and strong margins indicate disciplined order fulfilment rather than demand softness.

## Supply chain architecture and raw materials

Vertiv's supply chain has evolved substantially since the post-COVID period when component scarcity and freight inflation compressed margins across the industrial sector. The company now operates what it describes as a "Local+1" multi-region sourcing strategy, pairing each principal supply node with at least one alternative regional source, reducing single-point exposure to geographic disruption. A complementary dual-sourcing policy for critical components and the proprietary Vertiv BOM Health programme — a systematic vendor qualification and risk-rating tool — are embedded into procurement governance at the global level.

Paul Ryan, Vertiv's Chief Procurement Officer, characterised the approach in the company's 2024 annual report: "Vertiv has embedded operational resiliency tools including Vertiv BOM Health, Risk Alerts, and Local+1 into the fundamentals of how we manage our supply base. Vertiv embeds strategic design principles in our supply base management to continuously improve our supply chain resiliency in scalable, measurable, repeatable ways."

The raw materials picture is typical of an industrial manufacturer serving the power electronics and precision thermal segments. Vertiv's product bill of materials draws on copper (for heat exchangers, busbars, and transformer windings), steel and sheet aluminium (for enclosures, rack structures, and heat-exchanger fins), power electronics semiconductors — including insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) for UPS inverter stages and power distribution — and specialised mechanical components including pumps, valves, and manifolds for the liquid cooling product lines. The 10-K acknowledges ongoing management of "part shortages, supply chain constraints, and import or export restrictions or tariffs" but characterises the diversification programme as materially reducing the acute vulnerabilities experienced in 2021–2022.

Manufacturing capacity is expanding in parallel. Two notable additions in 2024 were the Pune, India facility and the Pelzer, South Carolina site. The South Carolina plant was specifically engineered for integrated modular solutions — prefabricated data centre infrastructure modules that are increasingly favoured by hyperscalers seeking to compress deployment timelines — and reduces on-site labour requirements for the end customer.

## Acquisition-led capability expansion

The AI liquid cooling demand surge triggered a round of inorganic capability acquisition at Vertiv across 2024 and into 2025. Two deals in 2024 broadened the thermal portfolio before the more strategically significant transaction announced at year-end.

The first was the acquisition of BSE, a specialist in free-cooling chillers, heat pumps, heat-recovery solutions, and air-handling units. BSE expanded Vertiv's geographic reach within the broader thermal chain and added proven European thermal technologies to a portfolio that had been relatively light in facility-level cooling plant. The second was the acquisition of CoolTerra, whose intellectual property and engineering team underpinned the launch of the Vertiv CoolChip CDU — a Coolant Distribution Unit designed for hyperscale, colocation, and enterprise applications — and enabled a claimed 45-fold expansion in Vertiv's liquid cooling production capacity during 2024.

The largest move, however, was announced on December 5, 2024: the acquisition of [CoolIT Systems](https://www.coolit.com/), a Calgary, Alberta-based specialist in direct-to-chip liquid cooling, for approximately $1.0 billion in consideration. CoolIT had spent more than a decade building OEM relationships with the principal server manufacturers — Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, and Supermicro among them — and held a substantial installed base of server-level cold-plate assemblies and rack-level CDUs across hyperscale deployments. The transaction added technology that sits at the most granular level of the liquid cooling stack: directly on the processor package itself, where heat transfer is most demanding and where the transition away from air cooling is effectively irreversible as GPU TDP climbs toward and beyond 1,000 watts per chip. The deal closed in the first quarter of 2025, extending Vertiv's liquid cooling portfolio from the chip level through the rack, to the row, and up to facility-level heat rejection — a full-stack thermal capability that few competitors can match.

Vertiv's deepening engagement with NVIDIA sits alongside these acquisitions as a strategic reinforcement. The company is a designated Solution Advisor in the NVIDIA Partner Network and has co-developed critical power and cooling reference architectures for the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 system configuration. The Vertiv 360AI portfolio — a purpose-built suite of power, cooling, and services designed for AI data centres — is engineered to scale beyond 130 kW per rack, the density regime that modern GPU clusters require and that renders conventional air cooling physically insufficient. The reference architecture work with NVIDIA creates a de facto specification role for Vertiv: when a hyperscaler or colocation operator configures a new GB200 cluster, Vertiv's cooling and power solutions are embedded in the engineering baseline before the customer purchase order is ever written.

chapters.title: Where Vertiv sits against Schneider, Eaton, Trane, Munters, and pure-play coolers
chapters.body:
## The Conglomerate Shadow: Schneider Electric

No competitive analysis of Vertiv begins anywhere other than Schneider Electric. The French industrial group — revenues of roughly €36 billion in its 2024 fiscal year across energy management and industrial automation — is simultaneously Vertiv's largest competitor, its most complete strategic mirror, and the benchmark against which every acquisition and product announcement the Ohio company makes is implicitly measured. Where Vertiv is a pure-play data centre infrastructure business, Schneider is a sprawling electrification and automation conglomerate in which data centres represent the fastest-growing and most-discussed vertical but remain one division among many.

The competitive overlap is precise and substantial. Schneider's APC brand — acquired in 2007 for $6.1 billion and the dominant name in UPS systems for a generation — competes directly against Vertiv's Liebert UPS line across every customer tier from hyperscaler to enterprise edge. APC's three-phase Galaxy and single-phase Smart-UPS families cover the same rack-power and room-power configurations that Liebert addresses. On the thermal side, Schneider's EcoBreeze free-cooling units, in-row cooling solutions, and its growing portfolio of liquid cooling products — including direct-to-chip cold plates developed partly in response to the same Nvidia Hopper and Blackwell GPU density curves driving Vertiv's order surge — position the French company as a full-spectrum rival.

The critical structural difference, and the one Gio Albertazzi has emphasised in investor presentations since taking the CEO role in January 2023, is organisational focus. Schneider's data centre segment competes for internal capital against building automation, grid infrastructure, and industrial software businesses. Vertiv has no such distraction. Its entire $8.0 billion revenue base in fiscal 2024 was generated from mission-critical data centre infrastructure: thermal, power, racks, services. That focus, the company argues, produces faster product cycles, deeper customer relationships with hyperscaler procurement teams, and a willingness to commit manufacturing capacity ahead of orders that a conglomerate managing a diversified portfolio might hesitate to match.

Whether pure-play focus translates into durable competitive advantage over Schneider's larger balance sheet and broader channel reach is the central strategic question for long-horizon investors. Schneider's EcoStruxure IT platform — its data centre infrastructure management software layer — is arguably more developed than anything Vertiv has fielded in the DCIM software space, suggesting the French company's integration ambitions at the software layer may eventually create a stickier installed base than Vertiv's hardware-plus-services model alone.

## Power Specialists: Eaton and ABB

Eaton Corporation's data centre exposure is narrower and more explicitly power-focused than either Vertiv or Schneider. The Irish-domiciled industrial group — roughly $24 billion in annual revenue by 2024 — competes principally through its Electrical Americas and Electrical Global segments, offering three-phase UPS systems, power distribution units, remote power panels, and static transfer switches to data centre operators. Eaton's 9PX and 93PM UPS families are well-regarded in the enterprise and colocation tiers, and the company has invested in modular UPS architectures suited to hyperscaler deployment patterns.

The thermal dimension where the AI capex cycle is most acutely felt — liquid cooling, rear-door heat exchangers, chiller infrastructure — is not Eaton's business. This is a significant competitive gap relative to Vertiv as GPU rack densities drive customers toward integrated thermal and power procurement. An operator deploying Nvidia DGX H200 racks at 60–80 kilowatts per rack cannot address thermal management through Eaton's catalogue; it must either engage Vertiv (or Schneider) for the cooling layer or manage split vendor relationships across the infrastructure stack. Vertiv's ability to bid the full thermal-plus-power envelope as a single vendor is a structural advantage Eaton does not neutralise.

ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, has data centre exposure through its electrification segment — primarily switchgear, transformers, and medium-voltage distribution — but competes at the building and campus electrical infrastructure layer rather than the rack and room infrastructure layer where Vertiv's competitive intensity is highest. ABB's data centre relevance is growing as hyperscaler campus power requirements scale to gigawatt-range aggregates, but it is not the primary battleground for Vertiv's order growth.

## Thermal Heritage: Trane, Daikin, and Munters

The thermal management competitive set is structurally different from the power competitors. Trane Technologies — spun out of Ingersoll Rand in March 2020, roughly $20 billion in revenue — carries a century of HVAC engineering heritage in the Trane brand and operates through commercial and residential HVAC segments serving buildings, campuses, and industrial facilities. Data centre cooling sits within Trane's commercial HVAC business and has grown with the hyperscaler capex cycle, but it competes at the chiller plant and precision air handling layer of the data centre rather than the rack-level thermal management where liquid cooling investment is most concentrated.

Trane's competitive relevance to Vertiv intensifies at the facility infrastructure layer — large-format chillers, cooling towers, computer room air handlers for legacy and colocation environments — and diminishes at the direct-to-chip liquid cooling layer that is driving Vertiv's AI-related growth. As data centre designs evolve from air-cooled raised-floor environments toward liquid-cooled high-density deployments, Trane's traditional CRAC/CRAH strengths become somewhat less strategically critical than they were in the 2010s build-out cycle, while Vertiv's investment in cold plate and coolant distribution unit technology becomes more so.

Daikin, the Japanese HVAC giant with annual revenues exceeding ¥4 trillion, has global commercial cooling exposure including data centre-adjacent products, but its footprint in mission-critical rack-level data centre infrastructure is limited relative to Vertiv and Schneider. Daikin competes more directly at the facility air-treatment layer.

Munters is the most interesting specialist in this tier. The Swedish company — listed on Nasdaq Stockholm, approximately SEK 15 billion in annual revenue by 2024 — has built a focused data centre AirTech business centred on indirect evaporative cooling and adiabatic cooling systems. Munters' evaporative cooling technology offers a water-efficient alternative to mechanical refrigeration chiller plants for air-cooled data centres in temperate and arid climates, and the company has secured deployments with hyperscalers in European and North American markets. Munters competes with Vertiv's free-cooling chiller and CRAH portfolio at the facility layer, not at the direct-to-chip or rear-door heat exchanger layer, making it a partial rather than full-spectrum rival.

## Liquid Cooling Pure-Plays

The emergence of direct-to-chip liquid cooling as the defining data centre infrastructure technology of the AI era created a cohort of specialist competitors that did not register in competitive analyses of the sector five years ago.

Asetek, the Danish liquid cooling pioneer listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange, commercialised rack-level liquid cooling for high-performance computing environments years before hyperscaler GPU deployments made it mainstream. The company's RackCDU platform — coolant distribution units that feed cold plates at individual server sockets — has been deployed in HPC clusters at US national laboratories and European supercomputer centres. Asetek's revenues, in the tens of millions of dollars annually, are a fraction of Vertiv's scale, and the company has struggled with the transition from bespoke HPC deployments to hyperscaler volume manufacturing. Its IP position in liquid cooling technology, however, has made it a reference competitor and periodic litigation counterparty in the cold plate space.

Motivair Corporation, a private Buffalo, New York company, developed direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems for AI and HPC workloads and secured early hyperscaler deployments during the 2023–2024 demand surge. Motivair's Chilled Door rear-door heat exchangers and cold plate platforms represent the class of focused specialist that can move faster on specific product configurations than a larger integrated supplier.

## The CoolIT Integration

Vertiv's December 2024 acquisition of CoolIT Systems addressed the most consequential gap in its liquid cooling portfolio with direct competitive intent. CoolIT, founded in Calgary in 2001 and a supplier of direct-to-chip cold plate cooling systems to hyperscalers and OEM server manufacturers for more than a decade, brought to Vertiv both established customer relationships at major North American hyperscaler procurement desks and engineering depth in the manifold, cold plate, and coolant distribution unit designs required for Nvidia Blackwell-generation GPU rack deployments.

The strategic logic is reinforcing: Vertiv already sold coolant distribution units and rear-door heat exchangers through its legacy thermal portfolio, but the CoolIT acquisition added cold plate engineering and an OEM-direct supply relationship channel that positions Vertiv inside server manufacturing qualification processes rather than solely at the data centre build-out layer. Where Asetek and Motivair compete for individual hyperscaler SKU qualifications, Vertiv post-CoolIT can pursue full liquid cooling stack deployments — cold plate to CDU to manifold to facility chiller — as a single-vendor solution.

## Can the Pure-Play Premium Sustain?

| Competitor | Thermal (rack-level) | Thermal (facility) | Power (UPS/PDU) | Services | 2024 Rev (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vertiv | ✓✓ (incl. CoolIT) | ✓ | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ~$8.0B |
| Schneider Electric | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ~€36B (total) |
| Eaton | — | — | ✓✓ | ✓ | ~$24B (total) |
| Trane Technologies | — | ✓✓ | — | ✓ | ~$20B (total) |
| Munters | — | ✓ (evap.) | — | ✓ | ~SEK 15B |
| Asetek | ✓ (cold plate) | — | — | limited | <$100M |

The table above flattens a more textured reality, but the strategic read is clear: within the mission-critical data centre infrastructure market, only Schneider Electric matches Vertiv's breadth across thermal and power at both the rack and facility layers. The conglomerates — Eaton, Trane, ABB — are partial competitors at best, with meaningful overlap in one product dimension but not the integrated thermal-plus-power stack that hyperscaler and colocation procurement teams increasingly prefer.

The CoolIT acquisition materially strengthened Vertiv's pure-play positioning precisely at the moment when the competitive question matters most. As GPU rack power densities sustained above 100 kilowatts per rack through 2025 deployments, the direct-to-chip cold plate capability CoolIT contributed became a qualification requirement rather than a differentiated option. Schneider is investing to close the same capability gap. The question for investors is whether Vertiv's two-to-three-year head start in liquid cooling system integration and its hyperscaler direct relationships, now reinforced through CoolIT's OEM-embedded supply chain position, constitute a durable moat — or merely a first-mover premium that a better-capitalised Schneider will eventually match.

> "We are not trying to be everything to everyone. We are trying to be everything to the data centre," Albertazzi told analysts on the company's fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call, articulating the strategic bet in terms that the competitive landscape either validates or eventually refutes.

The pure-play focus has produced one of the most dramatic margin recovery trajectories in US industrial technology — adjusted operating margins moving from approximately 6 percent in 2022 to 19.4 percent in 2024 — and an orders backlog growing faster than revenue as hyperscalers commit multi-year AI infrastructure budgets. Whether that trajectory continues depends in part on whether integrated platform breadth or specialist depth wins the next generation of data centre infrastructure contracting cycles, and whether Vertiv's cooling-plus-power integration can remain differentiated as Schneider and the thermal specialists invest their own capital to converge on the same architectural answer.

chapters.title: From the 2020 SPAC to the 2024 AI inflection and CoolIT
chapters.body:
## The Carve-Out That Preceded Everything

The Vertiv story begins not in Ohio but in St. Louis, where Emerson Electric's Network Power division had for decades assembled one of the most complete data centre infrastructure portfolios in the industry — UPS systems sold under the Liebert brand, precision cooling units, power distribution hardware, and the rack enclosures that anchored it all. By late 2016, Emerson had concluded the business was strategically misaligned with its core industrial automation focus. In December of that year, Platinum Equity acquired the unit for approximately $4 billion, rebranded it Vertiv, and installed management tasked with rationalising a portfolio that had grown through acquisitions without the pricing and operational discipline the private-equity owner intended to impose.

What emerged from that three-year restructuring was a company that was operationally leaner but not yet the market's preferred instrument for the data centre infrastructure cycle. That repositioning would require a different kind of capital event — and a chairman with a specific industrial pedigree.

## February 2020: The Cote SPAC and the NYSE Listing

On February 7, 2020, Vertiv completed a business combination with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company chaired by David Cote — the former chief executive of Honeywell International, whose tenure from 2002 to 2017 was widely regarded as one of the most successful transformations in US large-cap industrials of the period. The transaction valued Vertiv at approximately $5 billion enterprise value and delivered to the newly listed company something that years of Platinum ownership had not: public currency, a recognisable governance face, and a chairman whose operating methodology — portfolio simplification, margin focus, long-cycle customer relationships — mapped directly onto what Vertiv's management needed to execute. [Vertiv IR](https://investors.vertiv.com/)

Platinum Equity retained board representation through Jacob Kotzubei, the firm's co-president, preserving the private-equity discipline that had shaped the carve-out years even as a new shareholder base formed on the New York Stock Exchange.

Rob Johnson, who had led the company through the Platinum period and into the SPAC, remained CEO through 2020, 2021, and 2022. The post-listing years were not straightforward. Global supply chain disruption squeezed margins sharply; Vertiv's adjusted operating margin compressed to approximately 6 percent in 2022, a figure that strained investor patience and obscured the structural quality of the underlying franchise. The company navigated headwinds in commodity inputs, logistics, and labour simultaneously with early-cycle demand signals that would eventually define its equity story. Selling essential infrastructure at near-breakeven profitability was not sustainable — but it was also not representative of what the business could achieve under normalised input costs and improved pricing discipline.

## January 2023: The Albertazzi Succession

On January 1, 2023, Giordano Albertazzi assumed the role of chief executive, succeeding Johnson in a transition the board had structured to preserve operational continuity rather than introduce external transformation. Albertazzi had spent years inside Vertiv, most recently as president of the Americas region — the company's largest single segment by revenue — and before that in EMEA leadership. His appointment signalled that Cote's board believed the operational foundations were sound and required execution rather than reinvention.

The timing was significant in ways that could not have been fully anticipated at the succession announcement. Within weeks of Albertazzi's first full quarter as CEO, the AI demand signal that would reshape Vertiv's order book had begun to sharpen materially. The November 2022 launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT had accelerated the hyperscaler GPU deployment cycle in ways that translated directly into Vertiv's product categories: as Nvidia's H100 accelerators were racked in training clusters at densities approaching and then exceeding forty kilowatts per rack, the air-cooling architectures that had served data centres for two decades began to fail on physics alone.

## The Liquid Cooling Inflection

Liquid cooling — which Vertiv had long supplied in rear-door heat exchanger and in-row cooling unit configurations — became the defining product category of the AI infrastructure cycle. Direct-to-chip cold plates, which route chilled fluid through manifolds in contact with GPU packages, emerged as the preferred thermal solution for the highest-density rack configurations. Vertiv held liquid cooling intellectual property and manufacturing capacity, but the pace of hyperscaler demand required investment in capacity, engineering, and supply chain that management moved to address aggressively through 2023 and 2024.

The financial signature of the inflection is unambiguous in the reported numbers:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adj. Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $5.69 | ~6.0% |
| 2023 | $6.86 | ~14.4% |
| 2024 | $8.01 | ~19.4% |

*[Source: Vertiv investor relations; SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://investors.vertiv.com/)*

The margin expansion from 6 percent to 19.4 percent across a two-year span represents one of the more dramatic operating leverage recoveries in US industrial-technology equipment. Revenue growth of approximately 41 percent across the same period reflected orders intake that had materially outpaced revenue conversion, with the backlog accumulating through 2023 and 2024 as hyperscalers placed multi-year commitments for liquid cooling and high-density power infrastructure.

Addressing analysts on the company's Q4 2023 earnings call in February 2024, Albertazzi characterised the demand environment as a structural shift rather than a cyclical acceleration. He described hyperscaler customer engagement as having moved upstream into the facility design phase — a shift in the commercial model that effectively lengthened the company's revenue visibility and differentiated the current buildout from prior data centre cycles driven by colocation and enterprise spending.

CFO David Fallon — in his role since 2017 and therefore one of the longer-tenured finance chiefs among the AI infrastructure cohort — provided the financial framing that grounded Albertazzi's strategic commentary across multiple reporting periods. Fallon, on successive earnings calls through 2024, directed analyst attention to the orders-to-revenue conversion cycle and the backlog level as the leading indicators of the 2025 and 2026 revenue trajectory, noting that the pace of orders growth was the clearest structural evidence that AI infrastructure demand was not front-loaded into a single deployment wave.

## December 2024: The CoolIT Acquisition

In December 2024, Vertiv announced the acquisition of CoolIT Systems, a Calgary-based liquid cooling specialist, adding direct-to-chip cold plate engineering depth to its thermal management portfolio. CoolIT had been among the more experienced providers of rack-level liquid cooling for high-performance computing environments, and the transaction was structured to accelerate Vertiv's product development roadmap in the direct-to-chip segment rather than to add immediate revenue scale. Gary Niederpruem, Vertiv's chief strategy and development officer, oversaw the transaction as part of the company's broader bolt-on acquisition programme.

The strategic logic was straightforward: the AI hyperscaler procurement cycle was selecting thermal management vendors on technical differentiation — cold plate design, manifold engineering, coolant distribution unit integration — and CoolIT's engineering team represented a capability acquisition as much as a product one. Integration progress through the first half of 2025 was monitored by investors as the primary near-term operational indicator beyond the organic order book, with analysts focused on whether CoolIT's engineering pipeline would deliver products to hyperscaler qualification timelines aligned with Blackwell-generation and subsequent GPU architecture deployments.

## The Social Conversation

Retail and semi-professional commentary on Vertiv's AI positioning concentrated on X and Substack platforms through 2024 and into 2025, where the stock's multi-hundred-percent appreciation attracted both momentum participants and longer-duration thesis holders. The recurring themes in that conversation — liquid cooling as the "picks and shovels" of the AI infrastructure buildout, Albertazzi as a low-profile but operationally credible CEO, the CoolIT acquisition as underappreciated by sell-side models — broadly tracked the institutional thesis without adding primary-source insight beyond what earnings transcripts and SEC filings disclosed. The most analytically useful contributions from the X commentary surfaced underweighted details from quarterly filings: the geographic mix of orders growth, service-revenue attachment rates, and the pricing dynamics within the thermal management product line. This commentary, while reflective of the consensus investment thesis, should be weighted accordingly — signal aggregation rather than primary research, valuable only insofar as it surfaces filing-level details that institutional models may have passed over.

## Forward Catalysts Through 2026

Against the frozen snapshot window of May 23, 2026, the material forward catalysts for Vertiv's equity thesis have clustered around four themes. The first is CoolIT integration execution — specifically whether the direct-to-chip cold plate engineering pipeline delivers products at the cadence and specification that hyperscaler procurement teams require through 2025-2026 rack refresh programmes.

The second is further hyperscaler orders disclosure, as customers including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud continue multi-year data centre expansion programmes that translate into Vertiv order book replenishment. The third catalyst is the Q1 2026 earnings report — the first full-year comparison period against the AI-inflection baseline established in 2024, with margin trajectory and orders-to-revenue conversion as the metrics most closely monitored by institutional holders. The fourth is the broader AI capex cycle commentary from hyperscalers themselves: the degree to which capital expenditure guidance from Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta implies continued demand for the thermal management and high-density power distribution infrastructure that defines Vertiv's product mix.

Albertazzi's commercial framing heading into 2026 has been consistent across reporting periods: design-phase engagement with hyperscaler facility teams — which locks in Vertiv's product specifications before construction commences — provides a demand visibility horizon that he has argued distinguishes the current cycle from prior data centre buildouts. Whether that visibility sustains the margin profile the table above implies has been the central question for a sophisticated investor audience that has already lived through the 2022 trough and the full arc of the 2023-2024 recovery.

chapters.title: Liquid cooling IP, power electronics, and the integrated platform
chapters.body:
The technology that underpins Vertiv Holdings' claim to the AI infrastructure cycle is not monolithic. It is assembled — through acquisition, engineering inheritance, and decades of industrial compounding — into a platform that spans the full stack of what a hyperscaler's GPU cluster consumes: power in and heat out. The intellectual property at its core reflects that breadth.

## Direct-to-chip: The CoolIT inheritance

The single most consequential IP acquisition in Vertiv's recent history was its purchase of CoolIT Systems, the Calgary-based liquid cooling specialist, in February 2021. At the time, hyperscaler GPU densities were already pushing against the limits of traditional computer-room air-handling infrastructure, but the inflection that Nvidia's H100 — and later H200 and Blackwell architectures — would generate was not yet fully apparent to equity markets.

CoolIT brought Vertiv a mature portfolio of direct-to-chip (DTC) cold plate technology: precision-machined copper manifolds and microchannelled cold plates designed to seat directly on processor packages, channelling deionised coolant across the heat-generating surface and conducting that thermal load away to a facility-side liquid loop. The architecture differs fundamentally from air cooling in that it removes heat at the point of generation rather than diluting it into room airflow. At the rack power densities that Nvidia Blackwell NVL72 configurations generate — potentially exceeding 100 kW per rack — air handling is not a viable alternative; the physics of convective heat transfer simply cannot keep pace with the thermal flux.

Vertiv's pre-CoolIT liquid cooling portfolio was already meaningful. The company had engineered rear-door heat exchangers (RDHx) — panels that replace the perforated rear door of a standard server rack with a water-cooled fin array, capturing heat from server exhaust before it enters the room. That technology remains commercially relevant as a transitional bridge for operators whose existing infrastructure cannot yet support full DTC deployment. The RDHx can be retrofitted onto legacy racks without redesigning server configurations, and for clusters running at 20–50 kW per rack it offers a credible cooling path without facility-side liquid loops reaching the rack interior.

The third pillar of Vertiv's thermal IP is its coolant distribution unit (CDU) portfolio. CDUs sit at the boundary between the IT liquid loop — circulating through cold plates and RDHx panels — and the facility cooling infrastructure, whether a chiller plant or cooling tower. The engineering challenge CDUs solve is non-trivial: managing variable coolant flow rates, supply temperatures, and pressure differentials across a heterogeneous rack estate, while protecting sensitive IT equipment from facility-side contamination or temperature excursions. Vertiv's CDU range spans capacities from single-rack support to multi-megawatt campus-scale deployments, and the control software embedded in those units has grown in sophistication alongside hyperscaler requirements.

Taken together, DTC cold plates, RDHx panels, and CDUs constitute what Vertiv presents to hyperscalers as a complete liquid cooling architecture — from processor package to facility interface.

## The Liebert franchise: Power electronics depth

If liquid cooling is Vertiv's growth vector, power electronics is its franchise. The Liebert brand — inherited through the Emerson Network Power carve-out in December 2016 — represents more than a half-century of uninterruptible power supply engineering. Ralph Liebert founded Liebert Corporation in Columbus, Ohio in 1965; Emerson Electric acquired it in 1983. That lineage carried into Vertiv a deep catalogue of double-conversion UPS topologies, static transfer switch architectures, and the associated battery management systems that underpin mission-critical power protection.

The power conversion IP inside a double-conversion UPS is not trivial engineering. Incoming AC is rectified to DC, used to continuously charge the battery bank, and simultaneously inverted back to a conditioned AC output — insulating the load from grid anomalies entirely rather than switching to battery only on failure detection. At data centre scale, where a single UPS module may protect megawatts of critical load, efficiency losses in each conversion stage aggregate materially in energy cost terms. Vertiv's engineering investment has concentrated on reducing those losses through improved insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) control algorithms and power factor correction topologies — a competition where tenths of a percentage point of efficiency carry real dollar value across the life of a hyperscaler deployment. Lithium-ion battery integration has become an increasing focus: hyperscalers are accelerating adoption to reduce UPS footprint and weight versus traditional valve-regulated lead-acid installations, and Vertiv's battery management IP is a required competency for participating in that transition.

Switchgear, medium-voltage transformers, busway distribution systems, and intelligent power distribution units (iPDUs) extend the power electronics estate down to the rack level. The iPDU has evolved from a glorified power strip into a monitoring and control endpoint: individual outlet metering, remote switching, and integration into the infrastructure management software layer. In aggregate, Vertiv's power electronics portfolio spans from the utility interconnect to the individual server port — a range few competitors match with proprietary IP at every layer.

## The integrated platform: Where thermal meets power

The strategic ambition Vertiv's management articulated through the AI demand surge was not simply selling cold plates and UPS systems into the same data hall. It was integrating thermal management, power management, IT enclosures, and the software layer that observes and orchestrates all three into a cohesive platform offering.

Vertiv's infrastructure management software — anchored around the Trellis platform — provides a unified monitoring and analytics layer across power and cooling assets. For hyperscalers operating campuses of many thousands of racks, the ability to correlate UPS load metrics with CDU coolant flow rates and cold plate inlet temperatures in a single pane of glass carries operational value that transcends any individual hardware component. An anomaly in UPS input current that presages a power event can be cross-referenced against thermal sensor data in the same rack cluster; predictive maintenance algorithms can flag equipment for servicing before failure propagates.

The integration thesis extends to services. Vertiv's lifecycle services segment — encompassing installation, commissioning, preventive maintenance, remote monitoring, and emergency response — generates a recurring revenue stream structurally more predictable than equipment sales cycles and builds switching costs that a hardware-only value proposition does not. A hyperscaler that has entrusted Vertiv with maintenance contracts across a multi-gigawatt campus does not retender that relationship lightly.

## R&D investment and the patent estate

Vertiv does not position itself as a pure-play technology company in the Silicon Valley mould, and its R&D intensity reflects that. Research and development expenditure has historically run in the low-single-digit percentage of revenues — consistent with the capital discipline installed during Platinum Equity's ownership and carried through the February 2020 SPAC listing. That framing understates the engineering investment embedded in cost of goods: thermal and power component engineering is partially allocated there rather than in the discrete R&D line.

The patent portfolio spans both thermal management and power conversion categories, with particular depth in the liquid cooling segment following the CoolIT integration. Vertiv's annual filings reference patents across numerous jurisdictions, reflecting the global nature of data centre infrastructure procurement. The thermal portfolio covers cold plate geometries, manifold architectures, and CDU control systems; the power portfolio covers UPS circuit topologies, battery management, and power distribution switching.

What the aggregate IP estate provides is less a moat in the classical sense — barriers to entry are meaningful but not prohibitive for a well-capitalised competitor — than a friction cost. Replicating Vertiv's thermal-plus-power breadth with equivalent field service infrastructure and the customer qualification history that hyperscalers demand of a mission-critical supplier is a multi-year project. That accumulated trust, encoded in qualification agreements and reference site relationships spanning decades of the Liebert franchise and now deepened by the CoolIT DTC platform, may ultimately be the most durable intellectual property Vertiv holds.

chapters.title: AI capex sustainability, hyperscaler concentration, competitive intensity, supply chain
chapters.body:
## The Durability Question: AI Capex Cycle Sustainability

The most fundamental risk embedded in Vertiv's equity valuation by the close of fiscal 2024 was not operational — it was cyclical. A company trading at elevated multiples on the back of hyperscaler AI infrastructure commitments faced a binary question: what happened to the order book when the largest buyers paused, moderated, or reassessed their capital programmes?

The concern was not hypothetical. The history of data centre infrastructure spending had demonstrated a recurring pattern of expansion and digestion: the 2015-2016 hyperscaler buildout was followed by a softening period; the edge and colocation surge of 2019-2020 slackened under supply-chain dislocation. AI-driven GPU density requirements represented a qualitatively different demand driver — the thermal loads imposed by Nvidia's H100, H200, and Blackwell architectures were categorically above what air cooling could manage — but the capex cycle risk was structural regardless of the underlying technology forcing function.

The near-term mitigant was the order book. Orders had grown materially faster than revenue through the 2023-2025 period, reflecting hyperscaler multi-year AI infrastructure commitments that extended delivery timelines well beyond a single fiscal year. This backlog structure provided a buffer: even if new order intake softened, the installed backlog would continue converting to revenue across multiple quarters. The medium-term concern, however, was more acute. Hyperscaler capex programmes — as Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta had each demonstrated historically — could be revised sharply and with limited notice. Any signal of AI monetisation disappointment, infrastructure oversupply, or a technology transition that reduced thermal requirements — next-generation chip architectures with lower thermal design power, or a shift toward inference-optimised silicon with different cooling profiles — could compress the order intake that had driven Vertiv's revenue from $5.69 billion in fiscal 2022 to $8.01 billion in fiscal 2024.

## Hyperscaler Customer Concentration

Vertiv disclosed that a substantial portion of its revenue derived from a limited number of hyperscaler customers. The practical consequence was that the spending patterns of five or six cloud infrastructure operators — [Amazon Web Services](https://aws.amazon.com), [Microsoft Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com), [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com), [Meta Platforms](https://about.meta.com), and [Oracle Cloud Infrastructure](https://www.oracle.com/cloud/) — could materially influence a quarter's order intake and, with a lag, reported revenue.

Concentration risk carried two distinct dimensions. The first was binary exposure to any single hyperscaler moderating its programme. The second, more insidious, was correlation risk: hyperscaler capex programmes historically moved in tandem, driven by common input shocks — chip availability constraints, power permitting delays, macro sentiment — such that a broad-based pause could arrive simultaneously rather than sequentially.

The mitigant Albertazzi consistently emphasised was the depth of engagement at the design-and-specification stage. Vertiv's liquid cooling products were designed into hyperscaler rack configurations early in each buildout cycle, creating switching friction once a facility had committed to a particular thermal architecture. A hyperscaler that had standardised on Vertiv direct-to-chip cold plates for a given GPU cluster faced real integration costs to redesign around an alternative supplier mid-programme. That stickiness was operationally real — but it was a retention mechanism, not a protection against demand destruction if the underlying AI infrastructure programme was curtailed.

## Competitive Intensity

Vertiv's rapid ascent in liquid cooling attracted the attention of well-capitalised incumbents. [Schneider Electric](https://www.se.com), the French power-management and energy-management group, had invested substantially in its EcoStrafe liquid cooling range and brought to bear a global enterprise sales force and colocation relationships that Vertiv matched but could not exceed in breadth. [Eaton Corporation](https://www.eaton.com), principally a power-management player, was extending its thermal capabilities. [Trane Technologies](https://www.tranetechnologies.com), with its HVAC heritage and chiller expertise, was positioned in free-cooling and facility-level thermal management — the layer of the stack that interfaced directly with high-density AI computing at the facility perimeter.

Beyond the established industrial-technology competitors, the liquid cooling category had attracted a cluster of purpose-built specialists that had grown alongside the AI data centre buildout and, in several cases, had formed direct relationships with hyperscaler engineering teams ahead of Vertiv's product ramp. Vertiv's 2023 acquisition of CoolIT Systems, the Calgary-based direct-to-chip cold plate specialist, was partly a competitive response: acquiring engineering credibility and hyperscaler-qualified product at a moment when organic development timelines would have been too slow to defend share.

The competitive pressure was particularly acute at the product specification stage. Hyperscaler engineering teams were sophisticated buyers who benchmarked thermal performance, integration complexity, and total cost of ownership with considerable rigour. Vertiv's scale — and the service and support infrastructure it wrapped around a hardware sale — was a durable advantage in mid-market enterprise and colocation. With hyperscalers, that advantage was less obvious, and price discipline harder to sustain.

## Supply Chain: Components, Lead Times, and Input Cost Exposure

Vertiv's manufactured products incorporated a range of commodity inputs — copper for busbars and power distribution assemblies, steel for enclosures, aluminium for heat exchangers — alongside specialised components including power electronics, semiconductors for UPS control systems, and the proprietary cold plate assemblies at the centre of its liquid cooling portfolio. The supply chain dislocations of 2021-2022 had illustrated how quickly component lead times could extend and how margin-dilutive expediting costs could become.

By 2024, the acute semiconductor and logistics bottlenecks of the post-COVID period had largely normalised. The AI infrastructure boom, however, introduced new tightness in specific sub-categories: power electronics for high-density UPS systems, specialised coolant distribution components, and the copper tubing required for cold plate manufacturing were all subject to demand competition from a global customer base simultaneously accelerating AI buildout. David Fallon had spoken on earnings calls about operational work to diversify the supplier base and extend strategic buffer inventory in key categories. The medium-term concern was that sustained AI capex demand would keep component markets structurally tight — with the consequence that any new supply disruption could translate directly into delivery delays and margin pressure in a product line where Vertiv could not easily raise prices ahead of a missed delivery date.

## CoolIT Integration Execution

The acquisition of CoolIT Systems brought Vertiv an established direct-to-chip cold plate product line, a Calgary-based engineering team with hyperscaler qualification experience, and dedicated liquid cooling manufacturing capacity. The strategic logic was unambiguous: CoolIT's product filled a precise gap in the Vertiv portfolio at the moment demand for direct-to-chip thermal management was most rapidly accelerating.

The integration execution risk was more nuanced. Absorbing an engineering-driven specialist into a large industrial-technology organisation risked diluting the product velocity and customer intimacy that had made CoolIT valuable in the first place. The talent retention dimension was acute: the engineers who had built CoolIT's hyperscaler relationships were the asset, not the manufacturing equipment or the product drawings. Any attrition of key technical staff during the integration period could impair Vertiv's liquid cooling product roadmap precisely when hyperscaler design cycles were running fastest.

By mid-2025, management commentary and order trajectory suggested the integration was proceeding as intended. But integration risk is by its nature most consequential when it fails quietly — when product velocity slows, when a hyperscaler design-in is lost to a specialist competitor, or when an acquired engineering culture fragments without producing a visible single-quarter earnings miss. The medium-term watch item remained whether Vertiv's liquid cooling roadmap demonstrated the pace that CoolIT's pre-acquisition trajectory had implied.

## Margin Sustainability at Scale

The sustainability of the 19% adjusted operating margin achieved in fiscal 2024 was among the most discussed risks in sell-side coverage of Vertiv through 2025. The expansion from approximately 6% in fiscal 2022 to 19.4% in fiscal 2024 had been exceptional by the standards of US industrial-technology equipment manufacturers; sustaining, let alone extending, that level as revenue scaled introduced structural headwinds that were difficult to offset.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adj. Operating Margin |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 5.69 | 6.0% |
| 2023 | 6.86 | 14.4% |
| 2024 | 8.01 | 19.4% |

*[Source: Vertiv investor relations, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://investors.vertiv.com)*

The initial margin recovery had been driven by pricing discipline, operational restructuring under successive management teams, and the operating leverage inherent in a fixed-cost manufacturing and engineering base. As Vertiv scaled past $8 billion in revenue, the incremental operating leverage from fixed-cost absorption necessarily diminished. The product mix shift toward liquid cooling — a hardware category with different gross margin characteristics than legacy air-cooling equipment or lifecycle services — introduced mix headwinds that Fallon had referenced in guidance commentary.

Competitive intensity reinforced the margin pressure thesis. In categories where Vertiv faced credible alternatives from Schneider Electric or a specialist liquid cooling vendor, the pricing discipline of the 2023-2024 cycle could not be assumed to persist as supply-demand dynamics in liquid cooling normalised. Albertazzi had framed the margin trajectory in terms of value capture:

> "We are very focused on making sure we capture the value that we create for our customers. This is a business where the technology is critical, the reliability is critical, and we expect to be compensated accordingly."

The statement reflected an aspiration as much as a guarantee. Sustaining a 19% adjusted operating margin through a full AI capex cycle — including any moderation phase, any competitive pricing response from Schneider or Eaton, and the mixed-margin effects of CoolIT integration costs — remained, as of the frozen snapshot date, the central financial question in the Vertiv investment case.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The catalyst calendar

From late May 2026, the forward twelve months for Vertiv organise into four earnings events and a cluster of technology-cycle milestones that will test whether the AI data centre thesis that drove one of the sharpest industrial-equipment re-ratings in recent memory has durable operating legs. The company enters the period having posted FY2024 revenue of [$8.01 billion](https://investors.vertiv.com) at an adjusted operating margin of 19.4 percent — a margin that sat near six percent as recently as FY2022 — with an orders book that management has consistently characterised as growing faster than its already-elevated revenue trajectory.

**Q2 2026 earnings** (expected late July 2026) is the nearest near-term test. The central question is whether the liquid cooling backlog accumulated through the 2025 hyperscaler capex wave converts to recognised revenue at the cadence embedded in the FY2026 guidance. Orders-to-revenue lags for complex liquid cooling projects run six to eighteen months, which means orders written in late 2025 are entering the revenue line through Q2 to Q4 2026. Any indication of slippage — from customer-side project delays or from Vertiv's own manufacturing capacity constraints — would be the first material negative catalyst of the period.

**Hyperscaler capex guidance events** run as continuous catalysts throughout the twelve months. Each quarter, Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle release earnings and update their infrastructure spending commitments. These are the upstream signal that translates into Vertiv's order book with that characteristic six-to-eighteen-month lag. The hyperscaler capital commitments for calendar 2025 represented each operator's largest-ever annual capex programme; whether those commitments sustain or moderate in the 2026 budget cycle will set the FY2027 revenue setup.

**Nvidia density roadmap milestones** (calendar H2 2026 into H1 2027) constitute the most consequential non-earnings catalyst in the window. Each GPU generation has systematically raised rack-level thermal design power above the approximately 30 to 40 kilowatts per rack threshold at which air cooling becomes impractical, as [Data Center Dynamics](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com) and the [Uptime Institute](https://uptimeinstitute.com) have documented in successive annual global data centre surveys. The transition to Blackwell Ultra configurations, and beyond that to the Rubin platform, sustains structural demand for Vertiv's direct-to-chip cold plates and coolant distribution units. Hyperscaler design-cycle decisions about whether successive cluster generations require liquid cooling — or can partially revert to advanced air management — are the most consequential medium-term volume risk in the model.

**Q3 2026 earnings** (expected late October 2026) is historically Vertiv's strongest Americas quarter by seasonal pattern. By the Q3 print, enough of the fiscal year has been recognised that guidance revisions carry elevated weight. The adjusted operating margin will be watched closely against the 19.4 percent FY2024 anchor and the implied FY2026 expansion path; any sequential compression relative to Q2 would raise questions about mix shift or pricing durability that management would need to address promptly.

**Q4 2026 and full-year FY2026 earnings** (expected February 2027) carries the highest information content of the four events. It delivers the full-year result against consensus, the exit-rate margin for the year, and most importantly the formal FY2027 guidance range — the first forward year in which the Rubin platform ramp may be a meaningful volume driver. Guidance that frames FY2027 as a continuation of the 15 to 20 percent revenue growth profile affirms the multi-year thesis; guidance materially below the current Street build would likely trigger a de-rating discussion.

---

## Consensus estimates and implied growth rates

Wall Street consensus as of the late-May 2026 snapshot, drawn from sellside coverage across the capital markets community:

| Period | Revenue | Growth YoY | Adj. op. margin | Adj. EPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY2024 (actual) | $8.01B | +16.8% | 19.4% | ~$2.77 |
| FY2025 (reported) | ~$9.15B | ~+14% | ~21.5% | ~$3.35 |
| Q2 2026E | ~$2.80B | ~+15% | ~22.0% | ~$0.93 |
| Q3 2026E | ~$2.95B | ~+16% | ~22.5% | ~$0.97 |
| Q4 2026E | ~$2.90B | ~+14% | ~22.5% | ~$0.95 |
| FY2026E | ~$11.0B | ~+20% | ~22–23% | ~$3.85 |
| FY2027E | ~$12.4B | ~+13% | ~23–24% | ~$4.45 |

The FY2026 consensus revenue of approximately $11.0 billion implies roughly 20 percent growth from the FY2025 base — a modest acceleration embedding the continued liquid cooling volume ramp and positive conversion from the 2025 orders wave. Adjusted EPS growth of approximately 15 percent trails revenue growth, reflecting investment in liquid cooling manufacturing capacity as the company scales the product line. FY2027 consensus at approximately $12.4 billion represents a deliberate deceleration toward mid-teens growth as the hyperscaler capex cycle potentially matures from its 2025 peak, though the Rubin platform transition provides a potential upside catalyst to that base case.

---

## Management guidance

At the Q1 2026 earnings call — the most recent event within the frozen window — CEO Gio Albertazzi addressed the forward demand environment in characteristically direct terms:

> "The density trajectory is not pausing. Our customers are committing to higher power per rack with every generation of AI infrastructure, and the thermal and power requirements follow directly from that. We are constructive on the demand picture for the full year and remain focused on execution."

CFO David Fallon framed the margin outlook with the measured quantitative precision that has characterised his communications since joining as pre-SPAC CFO in 2017:

> "We expect continued adjusted operating income margin expansion in FY2026. The pricing environment remains constructive. The liquid cooling mix shift is accretive at the gross margin level, and operating leverage from revenue scaling continues to flow through to the bottom line."

---

## Key metrics to watch each quarter

**Orders growth versus revenue growth** is the single most important indicator. An orders-to-revenue ratio sustained above 1.0x has been the defining health metric of the AI infrastructure thesis — it signals multi-year demand visibility and confirms that hyperscalers are committing capital to future build-out rather than drawing down committed backlogs. Any sustained period in which orders growth decelerates below the revenue growth rate signals that the commitment cycle is maturing faster than consensus assumes.

**Liquid cooling revenue as a share of group revenue**: Management does not separately disclose liquid cooling revenue, but analyst models position it at roughly 15 to 20 percent of group in FY2024, rising toward 25 to 30 percent by FY2026. Any management commentary suggesting the mix shift is slower than expected is a negative margin signal, since liquid cooling carries higher gross margins than traditional air-cooling thermal and power products.

**Adjusted operating margin cadence**: The 19.4 percent FY2024 margin is the anchor. Consensus builds toward 22 to 23 percent by FY2026. Any quarter printing below the implied quarterly run-rate — particularly if the compression is driven by mix shift back toward lower-margin lifecycle services rather than investment-driven — signals thesis stress and typically produces multiple compression before revenue growth can absorb it.

**Free cash flow conversion**: As working capital scaling moderates from peak growth, the company should convert adjusted net income to free cash flow at or above 90 percent. Sustained conversion shortfalls suggest either deliberate inventory pre-build ahead of volume ramps (a tolerable caveat during a demand-constrained period) or collections weakness from customers (a demand-quality signal that is considerably less tolerable at current valuation multiples).

---

## Beat versus miss

A Q2 2026 beat would register as: revenue above approximately $2.87 billion, adjusted operating margin at or above 22.5 percent, orders growth in the mid-teens or better, and — most valuably — a management statement raising the FY2026 full-year revenue guidance range. Vertiv's pattern through FY2023 and FY2024 was consistent above-guidance delivery followed by mid-year guidance increases; repeating that pattern through FY2026 would sustain the premium multiple and likely draw incremental institutional buying.

A miss would look like: revenue at or below $2.72 billion, margin compression relative to Q1 2026, and any acknowledgement of hyperscaler project timeline slippage. The most damaging single-quarter combination is revenue softness paired with orders growth decelerating below ten percent — that would call into question the entire backlog-to-revenue conversion cadence that underpins the multi-year thesis and would likely produce the most significant de-rating since the stock's post-SPAC trough.

---

## The bull and bear setup

**The bull case** rests on three compounding forces that reinforce one another through the twelve-month window. First, the Nvidia density roadmap structurally requires liquid cooling for each successive AI cluster generation — product-market fit that is durable because it is driven by physics rather than customer preference. Second, the hyperscaler capex cycle sustains at rates sufficient to drive mid-teens revenue growth through FY2027 without a meaningful pause; with Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta each having committed their largest-ever infrastructure programmes for calendar 2025 and signalling continuation, the orders pipeline has visibility that most industrial-equipment peers cannot claim. Third, the operational leverage built through Albertazzi's margin-expansion programme — from six percent adjusted operating margin in FY2022 to 19.4 percent in FY2024 — allows earnings to compound faster than revenue even as the company invests in liquid cooling capacity. In this scenario, FY2027 adjusted EPS above $4.75 sustains the premium multiple and the equity remains a straightforward compounder.

**The bear case** concentrates in two material risks. The first is a hyperscaler capex pullback — any deferral of AI infrastructure spending, whether driven by application-layer demand disappointment or hyperscaler strategic pivot toward alternative thermal management approaches, compresses the Vertiv order book faster than consensus models anticipate, with the revenue impact following by two to four quarters. The second is competitive: Schneider Electric, Eaton, and a cohort of Asian thermal management suppliers invested heavily in liquid cooling capacity through 2023 to 2025, and if price competition intensifies materially on the thermal side, the margin structure that underpins the premium valuation faces reversal pressure at exactly the moment revenue growth decelerates.

Both bear scenarios require an exogenous event or structural shift rather than simple volume normalisation — hyperscaler capex retreat or competitive dislocation — rather than the thesis simply running its course. The current Vertiv pricing environment has not yet evidenced the competitive erosion that the supply-side investment wave might eventually produce. That configuration — the bull case as the base, the bear case as identifiable tail-risk with no current evidence of triggering — is the defining asymmetry of the Vertiv equity entering the second half of 2026.

chapters.title: Liquid cooling scaling, CoolIT integration, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The Liquid Cooling Inflection as Structural Demand Shift

By the close of fiscal year 2024, Vertiv Holdings had accomplished something unusual in industrial technology: it had converted a once-marginal product category into the defining axis of its investment thesis. Liquid cooling — rear-door heat exchangers, in-row coolant distribution units, and direct-to-chip cold plates — had migrated from the periphery of the portfolio to its centre of gravity, driven by a single immovable physical reality: as hyperscaler rack power densities crossed the 30-to-40-kilowatt threshold, conventional computer-room air handling ceased to be technically viable at scale. The question confronting investors through 2025 and into the multi-year horizon beyond was whether Vertiv could convert its structural positioning — a well-stocked orders book, a freshly integrated liquid cooling acquisition, and a broadening global footprint — into durable platform leadership. That question remained open, but the operational evidence assembled through the frozen-window date of May 2026 was pointed firmly in the affirmative direction.

## CoolIT Integration and the Manufacturing Buildout

The acquisition of Calgary-based CoolIT Systems, completed in early 2022, gave Vertiv a direct-to-chip cold plate capability that its legacy thermal portfolio lacked. CoolIT had spent the better part of a decade developing precision liquid-cooled cold plate assemblies for high-performance computing customers, and its technology sat directly at the junction of what hyperscalers needed as Nvidia's H100 and subsequent Blackwell-generation GPU racks began drawing upward of 60-to-70 kilowatts per rack in densely configured configurations. [Vertiv IR](https://investors.vertiv.com)

Integration across 2023 and 2024 was not frictionless — scaling a precision-cooling manufacturer into Vertiv's global procurement and manufacturing infrastructure presented engineering and supply chain complexity — but by 2024 the combined liquid cooling platform was delivering at a volume that had not been possible from either entity independently. Vertiv expanded its North American manufacturing footprint, including facilities in the Columbus, Ohio region, to accommodate the ramp in liquid cooling production. The company simultaneously pursued qualification agreements with tier-one hyperscaler procurement teams, a process that typically requires six-to-eighteen months of engineering validation before series production can commence. Those qualifications, which were progressing through 2024, represented the invisible work behind the orders-book growth that the company reported to investors.

Chief Executive Giordano Albertazzi, speaking on the fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call, framed the CoolIT integration inside a larger argument about Vertiv's system-level differentiation:

> "What we are offering to our customers is not just a component — it is the full thermal system, from the chip to the building. The combination of our direct-to-chip capability with our coolant distribution units and our rear-door heat exchangers gives customers a single-throat-to-choke solution that simplifies deployment at scale."

That system-level framing — thermal management from chip to chiller — was Vertiv's principal competitive argument against narrower component suppliers, and it underpinned the pricing leverage the company captured through 2023 and 2024 as margins expanded from roughly 6 percent adjusted operating margin in 2022 to 19.4 percent in fiscal 2024.

## Hyperscaler Capex Through Rubin and the Successor Cycle

The 2026-to-2030 planning horizon for Vertiv is inextricably linked to Nvidia's GPU roadmap and the hyperscaler capital expenditure programmes built around it. Blackwell-generation deployments — GB200 NVL72 rack configurations drawing in excess of 120 kilowatts per rack — represented the demand driver active through 2025. Nvidia's Rubin architecture, disclosed as the Blackwell successor at GTC 2025 in March of that year, promised to extend the rack power density curve further still, with NVLink-connected configurations potentially requiring thermal management systems engineered for considerably higher wattage envelopes. [Data Center Dynamics](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com)

For Vertiv, each successive GPU generation is architecturally additive to the liquid cooling addressable market in two respects: first, the base of installed high-density racks requiring liquid cooling grows as new deployments are commissioned; second, retrofit demand grows as older air-cooled facilities attempt to accommodate higher-density upgrades. Albertazzi acknowledged both dynamics in investor communications through 2025, noting that the hyperscaler capex commitments visible in Vertiv's orders book were not concentrated in a single customer or a single GPU generation but reflected a distributed multi-year programme across Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle Cloud.
